title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion to New Mexico in data privacy ruling
summary: A jury found that the social media company had deceived consumers for years about its data privacy policies.
story: Meta has been ordered by a judge in New Mexico to pay $25 billion to the state after a jury found that the social media company deceived consumers for years about its data privacy policies.

Judge Francis Mathew handed down the amount, which New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez described as "one of the largest, if not the single largest state verdict against a company in American history."
"This judgment should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley," Torrez said in a news conference.

In September, jury members found that Facebook had made false or misleading statements by telling consumers that they controlled how their information was shared. The social media giant also misled consumers by claiming it didn't sell or share personal information with advertisers, the jury concluded.

The jury found that the company's "most senior leadership," including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and former chief operating officer Sheryl Sandberg, made misrepresentations about the service's data privacy policies, the judge ruled.
"These communications were part of a coherent strategy designed to mislead the public," Mathew wrote.

The case stemmed from allegations that Facebook deceived users about a data breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, to generate targeted ads.
In a statement on Wednesday, Torrez said that the case "has always been about more than one company or one scandal."
He added, "It is about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences."
C.J. Mahoney, Meta's Chief Legal Officer, said in a statement that the company is confident it will "prevail on appeal."

"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."
Where the $25 billion could go
Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violations of consumer protection laws are funneled toward state education spending.
"We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years," Torrez said, while noting that the money would be tied up if Meta appeals the decision, as expected.
Forty-eight other states settled with Facebook in a nationwide case, but New Mexico chose to take the social media company to court on its own.
Attorneys for New Mexico had sought $35 billion to $40 billion, arguing that the company would only change its ways with a sum large enough to affect its stock price.
Lawyers for Meta said the company should pay no more than $3.4 billion, arguing that a much larger award would violate due process, be unconstitutional and not hold up on appeal.
In 2019, the Federal Trade Commission hit Facebook, then called Meta, with a $5 billion fine over its role in allowing Cambridge Analytica to collect users' data without their consent.
Meta argued that New Mexico failed to prove that the tech giant's executives made misleading statements about privacy and that its content moderation practices harmed state residents.
Shares of Meta rose $13.56, or 2%, to $707.81 in Wednesday afternoon trading.

title: Electricity bills force 1 in 5 to cut back on food, survey finds
summary: Americans living on a fixed income are particularly vulnerable when electricity costs surge, a Consumer Reports expert says.
story: About one in five Americans say they have had to cut back on groceries to afford their electricity bills, while roughly a quarter of consumers are turning down their heating or air conditioning to uncomfortable levels to lower their energy costs, according to a new survey from Consumer Reports.

About 80% of people who have lived in the same home for at least three years say their electricity bills have increased over that time, according to a national survey of more than 2,000 adults by the nonprofit advocacy group. The largest share, 28%, said their bills had surged between 20% and 49% over that period.
Electricity prices across major U.S. cities have jumped 14% over the last three years, according to federal data.

Rising utility costs are worsening the affordability crunch facing millions of American families, who are facing sharply higher gasoline and diesel prices amid higher oil costs due to the war in Iran. The survey found that consumers are cutting back where they can, such as switching to less expensive foods or spending less on discretionary items, to cope with rising electricity bills.

"We're hearing a lot of folks who don't know what they can possibly do to afford rising [electricity] rates," Sara Enright, senior director of safety and energy at Consumer Reports, told CBS News. "Vulnerable populations like students and retirees who live on a fixed income don't have a lot of flex in their budgets, and so when they get a surprise bill in the heat of the summer, it can be frightening."
Consumers often prioritize paying their utility bills because they need to keep their lights on and their refrigerators running, she added.
"People are cutting back on food" to pay their utility bills, Enright said. "They're definitely cutting back on non-essentials like vacations and eating out."

Other polls show that energy costs are weighing on voters ahead of next month's midterm elections, along with other cost-of-living issues. The cost of food is the top concern for voters in battleground states, followed by gas prices and utility bills, according to an October survey from Climate Power, a clean energy advocacy group.
"Increasingly distrustful"

Consumer Reports found that Americans blame their higher electric bills on utility companies seeking to maximize profits and on the rapid buildout of data centers. Electricity demand is forecast to increase 16% by 2029, mainly due to the proliferation of data centers across the U.S., according to energy management company Schneider Electric.

The price of natural gas, ongoing electrification of buildings and vehicles, and other factors are also contributing to rising power costs. Meanwhile, a majority of respondents said they don't believe state utility regulators are protecting their interests, Consumer Reports found.

"The public is becoming increasingly distrustful that government is looking out for them, and this is true across party lines," Enright told CBS News. "Everyday people, as the cost of living is rising, are concerned that their needs and interests are not being centered by the politicians and legislators that are supposed to represent them."

As electricity prices spike, more middle-income households are applying for government energy assistance despite their incomes being too high to qualify, Mark Wolfe, executive director of the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, told CBS News. The federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program is limited to people who earn less than 60% of their state's median income.

"People are dealing with high food bills, high gasoline bills, and they've just gone through high summer cooling bills," he said. "If you're living on a tight budget, from paycheck to paycheck, then the cost of driving goes up by $100, $150 a month, that might be the whole surplus in your budget."
Consumers "feel the government's not standing behind them, and they can't control these prices," Wolfe added.
Help decoding your energy bill

Consumer Reports said it's launching a new initiative called Power Smarter to help households reduce their energy costs. The effort includes a service called the CR Bill Decoder, where consumers can submit their electric bills. Consumer Reports, which will anonymize the bill data, will use the information to analyze trends and map prices across the U.S.

Bill Decoder "is intended to be a simple first step for anybody who wants to learn more about their energy bill and how they can take more power over their bill," Enright said. "We anonymize it and aggregate the data that we collect from it, and we'll be doing national-level and state-level evaluations of what's driving energy costs, and using that information to advocate for the American consumer to keep energy costs affordable."

title: Musk says SpaceX-Tesla merger has "a lot of merit." Here's why.
summary: Combining SpaceX and Tesla, whose stocks jumped after Musk said the companies are exploring a deal, would be the biggest corporate merger of all time.
story: Elon Musk on Tuesday said SpaceX and Tesla are exploring a merger — a business combination that one Wall Street analyst said could be worth nearly $5 trillion, which would make it the largest deal in corporate history.

"Both SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss this idea at the request of shareholders, and these special committees consist of independent directors," Musk said during SpaceX's earnings call with investors, adding that he sees "a lot of merit to combining the companies."
Tesla's stock price rose $14.01, or 3.8%, to $387.72, while SpaceX shares jumped $14.62, or 9.9%, to $162.41 in morning trading. Here's what to know about a possible merger between the companies.
How big would a SpaceX-Tesla merger be?
The merger would likely be valued at close to $5 trillion, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at investment firm Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News.

SpaceX is currently valued at $1.98 trillion, while Tesla's market capitalization stands at about $1.5 trillion. But Tesla shareholders would likely demand a premium for their shares to agree to the merger, Ives noted.
"For the merger to get passed by shareholders, it would have to be a higher price for Tesla — likely in the $500/$550 per share range in our view," he said.

That would make the combined company one of the most valuable in the world, rivaling that of the most highly valued businesses like chipmaker Nvidia, worth $5.2 trillion, or Apple, valued at $4.95 trillion.
What is the strategic rationale for merging the companies?

The main reason for combining SpaceX, a space exploration and AI company, with an electric vehicle manufacturer is to position them for a future in which artificial intelligence, or what Musk terms "super intelligence," becomes increasingly essential to everyday life.

"There's a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing super intelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass to orbit with the Starmind constellation," Musk said in Tuesday's earnings call.

While Tesla's primary business remains manufacturing EVs, Musk has signaled that the company is shifting away from traditional motor vehicles. In January, the Tesla CEO said the company would phase out production of its Model S and Model X vehicles.

Instead, the company is changing course to focus on developing autonomous products, such as self-driving taxis and humanoid robots. Musk said Tesla will eventually produce 1 million humanoid robots a year as the company transitions to an "autonomous future." The humanoid robot, called Optimus, could hit the market in 2027, Musk said in January.
AI is essential to Optimus, allowing it to follow orders and take on various tasks, as well as to Tesla's push into self-driving robotaxis.

Meanwhile, SpaceX owns xAI, Musk's AI unit that created Grok, the chatbot that is used in the social media app X and other Musk-owned products. Musk's planned Terafab chip factory will tie all the businesses together by manufacturing semiconductors for both SpaceX and Tesla.
Combining the businesses makes sense for a "number of strategic AI and data-driven reasons, and this is the right move for Musk," Ives said in a research note.
What are the hurdles to a merger?
On Tuesday's conference call, Musk underlined that a merger of SpaceX and Tesla is far from assured, noting that a majority of Tesla shareholders would need to vote in favor of the combination.
"I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it," he said.

Musk added, "At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this, and particularly on the Tesla side, we will need a 50% vote of all shares, not just those who vote, but of all shareholders. And that's quite a high hurdle to try to achieve."
Even so, Ives assigns an 80% to 90% chance that the merger will happen by the end of 2027.

title: Should you trust personal AI agents? What security experts say.
summary: The more access you give personal AI agents, the more capable they can be. But should you trust them?
story: Cybersecurity expert Hed Kovetz would love to have a personal AI agent handle some of his administrative tasks and lighten his workload. But he doesn't trust any of the commercially available agents, like Meta's Muse or OpenAI's Dots, with access to his email accounts, banking details, health records and other sensitive information.

"It's tempting to use a personal AI assistant. They access your email, order stuff and pay your bills. I would love to get that kind of help," he told CBS News. "But they could be taken advantage of or decide to go beyond the scope of what they are told to do."

While Kovetz sees tremendous commercial value in such products, he believes leading technology firms rushed them to market without sufficient security measures. For that reason, he advises consumers to be discreet about what they share with personal AI agents. Yet other AI security experts advise that consumers can use the tools as long as they rely on safeguards and are aware of the risks of providing personal data to an AI agent.

"I would be careful about giving full access to some of these commercial AI agents," Kovetz said. "I am aware of the fact that their security and privacy are far from being ready. Some consumers say, 'I don't care, I don't have anything to hide.' But that's not true; they still have medical records, bank accounts."

Such agents are already tremendously popular among consumers. When Meta's Muse first became available last month, it quickly became the most downloaded product in Apple's App Store. But while AI agents promise to save consumers time and even money by reading private correspondence and spending money on a user's behalf, they could also take actions that a user never explicitly authorized, leaving the user with limited recourse.

For example, it may be hard to know whether your AI agent is working for you or a retailer, Lindsay Owens, a consumer protection expert, told CBS News. She noted that Walmart's shopping agent, named Sparky, boosted average consumer basket sizes by almost 40% compared to shoppers who browse normally. Such data suggests that some AI agents could be trying to upcharge their users, she said.
Here's what security experts say they would and wouldn't let an AI agent do for them.
Should you let an AI agent shop for you?

Lynette Owens, a consumer education expert at TrendLife, an organization formed to protect households in the age of artificial intelligence by informing them about its capabilities and risks, also warned consumers against entrusting personal AI agents with too much access and information about them.
When it comes to online shopping, she believes AI agents can be extremely useful for researching products and comparing deals, but she cautions against letting them spend money.

"If you want to offload something like comparing deals, that's OK, but I'm not ready to hand off agency around a purchase, especially a high-ticket one. I wouldn't let it use my credentials like a credit card," she said.

One reason why she doesn't trust any commercially available AI agent to roam the internet with her credit card in hand is that criminals could trick it. Using what's called a "prompt injection," cybercriminals can trick an AI agent into ignoring its original instructions, such as "Don't spend more than $25."

Unlike traditional cyberattacks, prompt injection doesn't necessarily require hackers to break into an account or install malicious software. Instead, an attacker can plant instructions in a webpage, email or document that an AI agent encounters while carrying out a legitimate task.
If the agent mistakes those instructions for commands it should follow, it could be manipulated into revealing private information or taking actions its user never intended.

"We've seen an increase in incidents of prompt injections, and criminals are getting more clever about how they're hiding malicious code on websites," Owens said. "We're so excited about these new capabilities, but with any new technology, the security piece always lags."
Media and technology attorney Douglas J. Wood said consumers are liable if they authorize an AI bot to shop on their behalf, and it misinterprets instructions or overspends.

"If you give an AI agent, e.g., Muse, credit card information, you are making the bot an authorized user with the power to act on it," he told CBS News. "If it exceeds your instructions and spends your money, the card issuer will argue you authorized the purchasing tool."
Under federal law, such an individual would not be entitled to loss protection, Wood explained.
"Since you can't pursue the AI bot for improper use (it is not an entity that can be sued), your only remedy is to cut it off," he said, adding that by then the harm will have already been done.
His advice to consumers is: "Don't be lazy."
"Shop the old-fashioned way with the card in your hands. Authorizing an AI agent to use your card is like giving a bank robber the vault combination and telling him to steal only $100," he said.
How much data are you sharing?

New York-based entrepreneur Chris Franco, founder of marketing firm Woodridge Growth, has taken the opposite tack. He said tech companies have been collecting consumers' personal data for decades for various uses, such as selling it to advertisers, who use it to better market their goods and services.

"We've been giving out personal data to ad platforms for the last 20 years, and all we got back was better ad targeting," he told CBS News. "With these agents, you're sharing information, but the benefits are greater. It's a trade-off, but it's a much better deal."

To be sure, he wouldn't feel comfortable giving a Muse, Dots or Instinct AI agent full rein over his life, and believes it necessary to give it strict instructions while also monitoring its behavior and activity.

He likened giving an AI agent his credit card details to a parent handing off an exclusive credit card for high-net-worth individuals to a teenager without parameters. Both would be unwise, according to Franco.

Franco also allows his personal AI agents, including Muse and Grok Bot, to comb through his Gmail inbox. He's tasked them with organizing his receipts into a spreadsheet so that he can manage — and cancel — subscriptions.
It's a task he'd estimate would take him hours to do manually, if he ever got around to it at all.
"In 10 minutes, it had found a few I wasn't using. I would have canceled them anyway, but this did it way sooner," Franco said.

He acknowledges that it has insight into his personal life, including sensitive family matters, but at the end of the day, believes that the benefits of giving AI agents great access to his life outweigh the risks.

"The upside and pros of giving it context, in my view, are so much greater than whatever sci-fi-like scenarios there are of it going rogue," he said. "I am comfortable with it having that knowledge about me, because it can help me meet my goals faster."
Ask how it works

Matt Fredrikson, a computer engineering expert at Carnegie Mellon and founder of Gray Swan AI, an AI security company, said he gives his AI agents a fair bit of autonomy but also closely monitors their activity, using tools his company builds.
"The consumer-facing agents meant for normal people aren't immediately transparent about what they're doing with your data," he said. "But you can ask for that info if you probe them."
Simply ask your agent for a plain-language summary of how it went about completing the tasks it handled for you.
He also likened outsourcing administrative tasks to an AI agent to hiring a human personal assistant, which comes with a similar set of risks.

"If you have a human assistant, you've built a relationship with them, and there's a reason why you hired them in the first place. You trust them with a certain level of authority and autonomy," he said.

Simultaneously, when working with a human personal assistant, you're engaging in conversation with them and asking them to explain their thought processes. "You have to do that with these agents as well," he said.
Columbia Business School psychology and computer science expert Sandra Matz also drew parallels between working with a human assistant and an AI agent.
"If you wouldn't trust another person to deal with your personal information and process it safely, I wouldn't trust an agent," she said.
She highlighted one distinct difference between AI and humans, though.

"What prevents humans from sharing things they know about you is that they might feel guilty or ashamed, or have a negative emotional response to breaking the trust you've built with them," she said. "You can train an agent not to violate your trust, but they may violate it because they don't have guilt."

title: Amazon to hire 300,000 workers for seasonal jobs this year
summary: The online retailer plans to sharply boost its hiring for the holiday season this year. Here's what kind of positions they're looking to fill and how much they pay.
story: Amazon said on Tuesday that it plans to hire 300,000 seasonal, part-time and full-time workers across the U.S. this holiday season, up 20% from the same period last year.
Holiday retail sales this year are expected to top $1 trillion for the first time, according to a forecast from the National Retail Federation.

In September, Amazon announced that it was boosting the minimum starting wage for full-time workers to $20 an hour, while average pay for full-time staffers is roughly $24 per hour, according to the retailer.

Seasonal workers earn an average of $20 per hour, according to Amazon. Starting in 2027, seasonal employees who work at least 30 hours per week will also be eligible for the same healthcare benefits provided to full-time workers, the company said.

title: Trump announces $8 billion in diesel relief for U.S. farmers
summary: The USDA said farmers don't need crop insurance to qualify and can prepare to apply by creating a Login.gov account.
story: President Trump said his administration will provide $8 billion in aid to farmers hurt by record diesel prices.

"Tonight I'm also pleased to announce that the Department of Agriculture will be launching a new Harvest Fuel Relief program, providing our farmers with $8 billion in support to offset diesel costs during this harvest season," Mr. Trump said at a rally in Kansas Monday night.
"When Republicans win, we will pass even more funding for our farmers. We love our farmers," he added.

Earlier this month, Mr. Trump also signed an executive order to ease limits on the tax-free use of red-dyed diesel, a move aimed at lowering costs for farmers and truckers. That came after a $12 billion aid package for farmers announced by the Trump administration in December.

Farmers have faced financial pressures from soaring diesel prices, which are used to run agricultural machinery. Diesel reached a record of $6.53 a gallon on Sept. 22, although it's eased slightly since then, with average U.S. prices now at $6.32 a gallon, up from $3.62 a year ago, according to AAA data.

"This $8 billion investment will help bring certainty to our farmers during this harvest so they can continue to feed our nation," U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said in a statement.

Farmers would benefit more from a resolution in the U.S. war with Iran, which would likely result in lower energy prices, Gbenga Ajilore, chief economist at the nonpartisan Center on Budget and Policy Priorities and formerly a senior adviser in the Office of the Undersecretary for Rural Development at the Department of Agriculture, said in an email. Ending the Trump administration's tariffs would also help ease prices for farmers, he added.

"The president's economic aid to farmers ahead of the midterm elections follows a pattern dating back to his first term: He imposes policies that harm farmers, then spends taxpayer money to offset the damage his policies create," Ajilore said.

The USDA said the plan, called the Harvest Fuel Relief program, will pay farmers to cover part of their estimated losses for the 2026 crop year, using a standard formula. The calculation will use planted acreage reported to the Farm Service Agency, estimated production costs and crop yields and prices from the USDA's World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates report.

The agency said it will announce payment rates for major commodity crops in November, with details for other eligible products to follow. Farmers won't need crop insurance to qualify and can prepare to apply by creating a Login.gov account linked to USDA.

The USDA estimates that net farm income will drop 2.6% this year as production costs rise 4.5%. Fuel and oil expenses alone are expected to jump nearly 30%, according to a September forecast by the agency.

title: Vucic concedes defeat in Serbia's parliamentary election
summary: Aleksandar Vucic, who denounced the oppositional student movement as a foreign-led attempt to unseat him, led with virtually absolute power for 14 years.
story: The long-serving strongman leader of Serbia, Aleksandar Vucic, conceded defeat on Sunday in an election that pitted him and his right-wing party against a diverse student-led opposition movement that spent two years protesting his government.

It was a seismic political shift in the Balkan country where Vucic, who had been endorsed by Russian President Vladimir Putin and who denounced the student movement as a foreign-led attempt to unseat him, led with virtually absolute power for 14 years.

High turnout and gathering tensions marked the highly contested parliamentary election that was a showdown between Vucic and his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party and university students who, accusing the government of corruption and dismantling democracy, had built a popular following across the country.

Serbia's 6.4 million voters were electing lawmakers to the 250-member Parliament. In conceding the election, Vucic said his party projects that his opponents, the youth-backed Students' List, will take between 135 and 140 seats while his SNS party will have around 105.

"The Students' List has won," Vucic told supporters at his party's election night event, though he blamed Serbia's independent media as well as alleged interference by unnamed European countries and an "American deep state" for the loss.
Vucic said that his SNS party won around 1.7 million votes compared to the Students' List, which he said took around 2.2 million.
Supporters of the Students' List immediately flooded onto the streets of Belgrade and other cities, honking horns, shouting and chanting: "Aleksandar is gone," referring to Vucic.
The outcome, which Vucic announced only around an hour and a half after polls closed, came after tensions had built as voting progressed during the day.

Police in anti-riot gear cordoned off an area in central Belgrade around the election commission headquarters. Special police vehicles could be seen near a Belgrade park where Vucic's loyalists have been camping for over a year, and large groups of black-clad men had congregated at various points throughout the city.
Vucic was seeking to become Serbia's prime minister after serving two near-full terms as president. He resigned the presidency last month to lead the campaign.

Support for the populist had eroded since 16 people were killed in 2024 when a concrete canopy collapsed at a train station in Novi Sad. That set off a wave of youth protests that blamed the collapse on high-level corruption, cronyism and rampant graft during renovation work at the station.

Despite the protests, Vucic retained considerable support among many of Serbia's voters. Admirers viewed him as a capable leader who can steer the nation through global uncertainties - the image that was carefully crafted by the mainstream media.

While the increasingly authoritarian Vucic has routinely outplayed Serbia's fractured opposition in the past, the leaderless youth movement proved to be a tough opponent that rattled his firm grip on power in Serbia like no one else in the 14 years since his party took office.

The newly formed Students' List movement was shaped by university students, but none actually appeared on the election list. Instead, its candidates are little-known experts, athletes, farmers and artists.

This approach was meant to counter Vucic's one-man rule and restore a sense of community and solidarity. The students' message during the campaign focused on a non-partisan effort to rebuild Serbia's economy and restore its democracy.

The students have used youthful energy to attract voters who are disillusioned with local politicians. Vilified by pro-government media, they cycled and walked through the country to reach voters in rural areas — Vucic's traditional strongholds.

The student victory echoed the recent electoral defeat of a Vucic ally in Hungary, where youth participation helped oust the autocratic Viktor Orbán after 16 years and bring in a new pro-European government. It was likely to resonate beyond Serbia as countries across Europe have faced angry youth and student protests.

Monitors predicted that total turnout in the election could reach around 70%, unseen in Serbia since 2000. During the day, long queues formed at polling stations in Serbia and in cities around the world. Some in the Serbian diaspora were made to vote in the middle of the night after authorities tied voting hours to local Serbian time.
Recent Serbian elections had been marred by irregularities, and the EU was closely watching the conduct of Sunday's vote in a candidate nation for the bloc's membership.
Independent election monitors reported dozens of cases of irregularities on Sunday such as photographing of ballots that suggested pressure on voters and attempted vote buying.

Both international and local election monitors had expressed concern about the safety and fairness of an election campaign marked by detentions, near-total government control over the media and reports of surveillance and cyberattacks against activists.

Local elections earlier this year in 10 municipalities in Serbia saw violent attacks on journalists and activists. The previous parliamentary vote in 2023 was followed by opposition protests alleging fraud.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So the DOJ lawsuit says the defendants, who are the state election board and the ballot-counting review board – quote – "not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion."

It's not saying, don't certify. It's saying, if a court ultimately determines that it was decided because of confusion and not the will of the voters, then we do not think the states should certify, and that's consistent with federal law and consistent with even Alaskan law, if that happens.

Eighty-three percent see it as a concern in determining their vote. And they see it as more of an issue with Republicans. How does your party overcome this perception?
SENATOR THOM TILLIS: Well, I think a part of what we have to do is be open about what we've done right and where we've kind of skated into the gray area.

I'll give you a good example of why I think maybe people feel that way. You can't have an oligarch pay tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars for the president's son's wedding and not make it look odd, particularly when that oligarch is aligned with Putin and has gone on delegations with Putin to Beijing. That's just one example.
What we need to do is learn the rule of, figure out where the line is and take a step back. Our American people are already predisposed to assume Democrats and Republicans are corrupt.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR THOM TILLIS: We're just feeding that narrative when we let things like that happen. Whether it's legal or not, it's irrelevant.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
Well, it seems Democrats may be carrying out some scrutiny if they do win the majority.

You will not be in the Senate at that time. You're retiring. And you were deeply frustrated by Republicans when they passed this tax and spending bill on a party line vote that included cuts to Medicaid and will deeply affect rural hospitals. In your state, more than 25 percent of people rely on Medicaid. I know North Carolina has tried to patch things up here to plan ahead. Do you still expect devastating healthcare cuts in the new year?

SENATOR THOM TILLIS: We're going to have significant headwinds. It's really a ten-year impact if you take a look at the original bill. And by the way, I supported the tax provisions of the bill. It was the healthcare provisions beyond what the House has proposed that are problematic. And it's going to take time.

What I was trying to do was not necessarily get rid of the cuts, but try to affect their timing. I think they're coming too soon. And I have a lot of experience with the state budget here in North Carolina, understanding Medicaid. I believe it's going to be very, very challenging. And we're going to have to get it – we've got our work cut out for us because some of those impacts could also feed right into the 2028 election.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So healthcare will be a big factor in that election is your prediction it sounds like. I want to ask you a bit –
SENATOR THOM TILLIS: Absolutely.

MARGARET BRENNAN: A bit about what I engaged with the attorney general on. In recent weeks, the Justice Department filed this case up in Alaska to preemptively challenge the outcome there. Out in California, DOJ also told election officials they'll risk, quote, "legal consequences" if they continue to send vote by mail ballots to a list of voters they say are not confirmed citizens. And then there was, of course, this action taken against Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, though she has not been charged with a crime.
Do you see a pattern here and are you comfortable with these actions this close to an election?

SENATOR THOM TILLIS: Well, I think we have to be careful. First, you've got to take them separately. California has been guilty of ballot harvesting. They have a policy to do it. They have a system there that is ripe for abuse. And they need to be looked at.

Alaska has a candidate who just coincidentally happens to be the same name as my friend and colleague who came in with me in 2014. And they also have rank choice voting. So, I think it's appropriate to take a look at it. I'm not sure why they thought they had to file a lawsuit other than, as Todd said earlier, make sure that you have the ballots right so we can be certain that the Democrats were not successful in confusing candidates to vote for someone else to better position Peltola for being the winner.

And with respect to Omar, I've got to look at the details there, but I found it very concerning. You know, as a member of Congress, you better have a very, very high bar to issue a subpoena and a search warrant. And the facts better be there otherwise the DOJ needs to be held accountable. It's that simple. I'd say the same thing if it was a – and I have in the past, in a Biden administration, where I felt like they were moving a little bit out ahead of their skis. They'd better have the facts to substantiate their action.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, I guess that gets to the timing of it all because the action itself draws attention and scrutiny of whether or not the cases actually have legs to them. But up in Alaska, your Republican colleague, Lisa Murkowski, the other Republican senator, said the DOJ should never have filed the lawsuit. She said when it came to the ballot, Alaskans don't need help picking a preferred candidate. The state already handled this by distinguishing the candidates on the ballot. And the Department of Justice should never have filed the lawsuit.
You sit on judiciary. I mean what are the consequences? Will there be any?

SENATOR THOM TILLIS: Well, there are very few people that know Alaska better than Lisa. To be honest with you, Lisa Murkowski is a friend and an extraordinary member of the U.S. Senate. I agree that I think the lawsuit – I mean filing a lawsuit before anything that could be substantiated, it's a legal question, is suspicious to me. I'm on Judiciary, but I'm not an attorney.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Even before the election is held.

SENATOR THOM TILLIS: Yes, that's what I mean. It's almost a preemptive, a presumptive posture versus simply telling the Alaska election officials, we're going to be watching this closely because clearly Democrats gamed the system by having a Dan Sullivan on the ballot. Either the Democrat Party, there's some evidence to suggest that Chuck Schumer may have even been involved. So, I don't mind looking at it, but I do mind the appearance of filing a lawsuit before we know if the facts that would substantiate a lawsuit actually occur.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, that Dan – other Dan Sullivan claims he's not a Democrat but there has been reporting that a Democratic strategist may have helped him along the way. But that is something that is –
SENATOR THOM TILLIS: It's a strange coincidence. We can all admit that.
MARGARET BRENNAN: It – no doubt. No doubt. But the state has handled it and clearly the senator thinks handled it well.

I want to get back to Vladimir Putin because you have been very vocal in recent days about your concern here with President Trump and his actions. Just yesterday Elon Musk said the SpaceX satellite services have been restored. And Senator Cramer of North Dakota, who was on this program last week, told us though he is concerned one person or one company just has too much control over America's ability to protect the domain of space.

You know, people might be confused over which service was switched on and off and to what degree, but the bigger picture issue here that your Republican colleagues seem concerned about is just how much control Elon Musk has over defense. Do you share that concern?
SENATOR THOM TILLIS: Yes, I do. And I have a concern with the whole narrative that played out.

Elon Musk – I was trying to put pressure on everyone to own responsibility for this. Elon Musk originally said he didn't do it. Then we start focusing on the administration and now we hear Elon says that he did.

And also, to the American people, many members of Congress, this distinction between Starlink and Starshield, are you telling me – and I agree with Kevin Cramer, he's a great senator also, are you telling me that we don't know something as important as a tool that's being used by our western nations is subject to the whims of one CEO and that there's some other, the Star defense, is that controlled by him? Controlled by somebody in DOD? We need answers to this question. And I'm not satisfied. I'm glad that the capability is back up. Shame on whoever is responsible for it ever having elapsed. People died in that intervening time.

But what I want to know more importantly is, what – to what extent is the Department of Defense and the U.S. government involved in this? I get it's a private company, but they're playing into military space, geopolitical space, that there's got to be some guardrails and accountability, in my opinion.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, I know you helped organize a call with Senator Blumenthal and President Zelenskyy this past week to try to get some clarity around this. From what you know, are all of the arrangements to expand access, to let Ukraine target inside of Russia? Is all of that on hold right now?
SENATOR THOM TILLIS: You know, the best we could tell – when we're thankful for doing nothing more than reestablishing the current capabilities, I am concerned that we're not expanding it.

Look, there is a bad guy and there is a good country in the mix here. The bad guy is Vladimir Putin. The good country is Ukraine. We, like the other western European nations, need to support them, expand capabilities and defeat Putin. Putin is no friend. There is no such thing as a win- win when you're dealing with a despot, a totalitarian in the western world. So, we need to plus up that capability, not simply be thankful for getting something back that was working fine two weeks ago, was working OK when I was in Ukraine just a month ago.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, in the back and forth over exactly what was turned off and why Russia was able to hit inside of Ukraine so much over the past ten days, it came to light that there were also failures of the early warning system. Two, if not three, the BC3 systems did not detect incoming Russian ballistic missiles into Ukraine. Secretary Rubio was asked about this and he talked about technical issues. That sounds deeply concerning. I mean does this mean that Russia can subvert American early warning systems, or are we misunderstanding that?

SENATOR THOM TILLIS: I think that's a legitimate question. That's why I think this whole timeline needs to be examined, probably in a – in a secure setting. Not necessarily in a public hearing. But we need to go through that entire timeline and say, seriously, guys, we're that vulnerable? I don't think we are.

And so, I'm beginning to think that maybe we're finessing around the reality that somebody needs to own the lapse in service and it became – it came at the same time the Starlink or Starshield capabilities went down.

Let's just map this out, folks. I don't mind – the American people don't mind people making mistake or maybe having a policy they decide they've to – they've got to reverse. We're an great nation – we're an exceptional nation, greatest nation on earth. This is a simple question. We should have simple answers for it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, we will continue to try to get answers.
Sir – thank you, Senator, for your time today.
SENATOR THOM TILLIS: Thank you.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And we will be right back.

title: Gina Hinojosa says there's "deep disappointment" in both parties
summary: Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat running for governor in Texas, said there's "deep disappointment in both political parties" in the Lone Star State.
story: Washington — Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat running for governor in Texas, said on Sunday that there's "deep disappointment in both political parties" in the Lone Star State, prompting a new path forward that she argued is "post-partisan in some ways."
"Right now nobody wants politics as usual. Most of us see that it is broken," Hinojosa said on "Face the Nation."

Hinojosa, 52, is taking on Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas. A civil rights and labor lawyer who's represented parts of Austin in the Texas House since 2017, Hinojosa would be the first Democratic governor and the first woman to lead the state in the governor's mansion in three decades. A recent CBS News poll had Abbott leading Hinojosa, 52% to 48%.

But in a state like Texas, which has more registered Republican voters than Democrats, Hinojosa will need support from both sides of the aisle to pull off a victory. She argued that the deep disappointment she described in both parties has made Texans forge "a new way forward."

"There is bipartisan anger about what Greg Abbott has done to our public schools," she said. "Saving Texas public schools is a key part of my agenda, and that's why this campaign has resonated amongst Texans."

Hinojosa said her agenda "is not a Democratic agenda," but rather a populist one aimed at delivering for Texans. She cited healthcare access for children and combating high insurance premiums as key focus areas.

She also pointed to data centers as an issue where Texans can find agreement. She said, "Nobody's pushing back against the data centers harder than MAGA because these data centers are mostly moving into our rural communities that are unincorporated."

"This part of Texas is being taken advantage of by these data centers, and the people of Texas and rural Texas are being taken advantage of," she said. "There are big water concerns, there are big electricity cost concerns, property rights concerns, and so we need to visit all of it and make sure Texans are protected, and first and foremost have a seat at the table."

The comments come as Hinojosa has filed a lawsuit to obtain emails between Abbott and Elon Musk, who's given millions to Abbott's campaign. She said, "We need to know what exactly is going on," pointing to the relationship between Abbott and Musk, the CEO of Texas-based Tesla and SpaceX.
The Democrat expressed optimism about her chances in next week's election, despite Texas being a reliably red state for over 30 years.
"Turnout is high, enthusiasm is high on our side, so we feel really good about where we are," she said.

title: Blanche says DOJ is "doing our own research" with Alaska challenge
summary: The Justice Department filed a lawsuit last week to preemptively challenge the certification of Alaska's Senate race if the Republican incumbent, Sen. Dan Sullivan, loses.
story: Washington — Attorney General Todd Blanche said Sunday that the Justice Department was looking to "put guardrails in place" with its move to prevent the Alaska Senate election from being certified if there is evidence that voters were confused by a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
"This is the Department of Justice doing our own research under the law," Blanche said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

The Justice Department filed a lawsuit last week to preemptively challenge the certification of Alaska's Senate race if the Republican incumbent, Sen. Dan Sullivan, loses. Sullivan is facing off against Democratic candidate Mary Peltola in next week's election, in a race that has appeared closer than initially expected in a state that President Trump won in 2024 by double digits. But the state has a top-four primary and ranked-choice voting election system, with another candidate adding a wrinkle to the race.

Daniel J. Sullivan, a former teacher who shares the same first and last name with the sitting senator, announced in June that he was entering the race, prompting a push by the incumbent senator to remove him from the ballot. That month, an Alaska election official determined he was not eligible to appear on the ballot, citing a "determined effort and a deliberate attempt" to confuse Alaska voters. But the challenger appealed the decision, and the state Supreme Court later affirmed that he could appear on the ballot, paving the way for both Sullivans' names to appear.

Blanche emphasized Sunday that the DOJ's lawsuit is "not saying, 'don't certify.'" But if a court determined that the race was decided "because of confusion, and not the will of the voters," then the Justice Department does not think the state should certify the election.
The attorney general argued that it may "be obvious from the results and from the ballots that voters were confused," though he acknowledged that "we don't know what's going to happen yet."

"That could be obvious from the way that they rank the Dan Sullivans, or not including a Dan Sullivan on the ballot, I don't know yet because there hasn't been an election," Blanche said. "But all we are doing is trying to put guardrails in place so that if that happens, there's a system allowed where the ballots are kept in a way so that we can determine whether there was confusion."

Pressed on why the challenge was filed 11 days before Election Day, Blanche said the administration had hoped that the state Supreme Court "would actually issue an opinion and explain their reasoning." He said that it's an issue the president has been talking about for months, saying, "This isn't something new that just came up last week."

Asked Friday about the Justice Department's lawsuit, Mr. Trump told reporters, "Well, I'm the one that said, 'do it.'" Blanche said he had "no idea" to whom the president was referring, and would not discuss his own personal communications with the president.
Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a Republican who also appeared on "Face the Nation" on Sunday, said he thinks it's appropriate "to take a look at" the situation in Alaska.

"I'm not sure why they thought they had to file a lawsuit, other than as Todd said earlier, make sure that you have the ballots right so we can be certain that the Democrats were not successful in confusing candidates to vote for someone else to better position Peltola for being the winner," Tillis said.
The comments came after GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski, Alaska's other senator, on Friday said she was opposed to the Justice Department's move.

"Alaskans don't need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year's ballot," Murkowski wrote in a post on X. "The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit."
The sitting senator's name will be noted as "(Registered Republican) Incumbent" on the ballot.
Asked about Murkowski's comments, Tillis said, "there are very few people that know Alaska better than Lisa."
Tillis said he doesn't mind "looking at it," but "I do mind the appearance of filing a lawsuit before we even know if the facts that would substantiate a lawsuit actually occur."
The Peltola campaign, meanwhile, has called the DOJ's move "a despicable political threat to overturn an election."

"We will fight to ensure every single eligible voter in Alaska can make their voice heard and that no bureaucrat or politician from the Lower 48 can interfere with our lawful, secure elections," said Peltola campaign spokesperson Harry Child.

title: Alaska Senate candidate sustains "minor injuries" in car accident
summary: Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola sustained "minor injuries" in a car accident, her campaign said.
story: Washington — Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola sustained "minor injuries" in a car accident, her campaign said Sunday.
"Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits," Peltola's campaign manager, Cheryl Bruce, said in a statement.

Peltola and her family were on their way to the Alaska Federation of Natives Annual Banquet when the vehicle transporting them was struck by another driver, her campaign said, causing injuries that required medical attention.
Bruce said at the advice of medical professionals, Peltola was rescheduling campaign events "as she takes time to recover."

"Mary is disappointed that the accident is delaying the start of her Alaska Always Tour, and she is eager to get back on the campaign trail to speak directly with Alaskans about her plan to take on the rigged system and lower costs for working families," Bruce said.
Peltola's events on Sunday and Monday would be rescheduled in the coming days, the campaign said.

Peltola, 53, is vying to unseat GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan to become the first Democrat elected to the Senate since 2008, four years after she became the first Democrat to represent the state in the House in 50 years . She was the top vote-getter in the August top-four primary, setting up the general election contest against Sullivan and two other candidates under Alaska's ranked-choice election system.
