title: Security cameras upend man's story of finding wife fatally shot in his car
summary: David Tolbert told investigators when he opened his car door outside a store where he was working in Huntsville, Alabama, he discovered his wife Savannah Tolbert's lifeless body in the front passenger seat. Investigators would rely on multiple security cameras to piece together what happened.
story: It was Tuesday, Nov. 15, 2022, and a small strip mall in Huntsville, Alabama, was teeming with police activity.
The frantic scene was captured on police body cameras and dashcam video in the moments after police discovered 37-year-old Savannah Tolbert shot dead in the front seat of a red Tesla.

Moments before police arrived, her husband David Tolbert was captured on video from security cameras in the store where he had been working -- after he found her lifeless body. He appeared shocked and upset and is seen walking briskly with his hand covering his mouth.
Moments later, David Tolbert is seen crouching on the floor. When police arrived at the scene, the store's owners said they observed David with tears in his eyes and his hands in his pockets.
Red flags appear early in Savannah Tolbert's death investigation
Jeff Kreiter and Greg Hayden, investigators with the Huntsville Police Major Crimes Unit, were assigned to the case.
Investigator Greg Hayden: We wanna know … who saw what happened … because … information is the most important thing that … we can get out there.
When Hayden arrived at the scene, it appeared that Savannah Tolbert had taken her own life.
Investigator Greg Hayden: She's sitting up … in the passenger seat with her head tilted … to the left side ...
Anne-Marie Green: Where is her hand and where is the gun?
Investigator Greg Hayden: The gun is in … her right hand. And it's actually laid across her lap.
First responders said they had found Savannah Tolbert's fingers curled around the gun when they got there.  It was a red flag for investigators.
Investigator Greg Hayden: It didn't match up to a suicide … her gun was in her right hand … and the bullet hole was on her left side in the back of her head.
None of it made sense to Savannah Tolbert's sisters, Holly and April Hancock.
April Hancock: No way.
Anne Marie Green: — your sister did this to herself.
April Hancock: Never. No.
Anne Marie Green: Why so sure?
April Hancock: She wouldn't do that. …
Holly Hancock: She wouldn't leave her daughter.
April Hancock: She knows – she — no.

In addition to the gun that police determined belonged to her, authorities discovered a shell casing on the rear seat, behind the driver. The Tesla was seized as evidence and taken by police for testing.
Anne-Marie Green: Who do you want to talk to next?
Investigator Greg Hayden: Our most important person is … her husband.
Anne-Marie Green: David is handcuffed and put in a patrol car. … he's a grieving spouse. Why was he handcuffed?
Investigator Greg Hayden: Our policy … is that whenever we transport somebody, if they are in … a scene, we always handcuff … for officer safety.
David Tolbert, 47, hadn't been arrested, but he was a person of interest. He was taken to the police station. Once the handcuffs were off, investigators began questioning him.
Investigator Jeff Kreiter: What we had to work with at that point is — who was around her.
Kreiter was joined by Investigator Julian Johnson, who had met David Tolbert at the scene.
INVESTIGATOR JULIAN JOHNSON (police interview): Hey David.
DAVID TOLBERT: Hey.
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: Remember me?
DAVID TOLBERT: Yes, sir.
On that day, David Tolbert, a retired corrections officer, was helping the owners of a new store prepare for a health inspection. After investigators read David his rights, he started talking.
Anne-Marie Green: What does David tell you happened that day?
Investigator Jeff Kreiter: He was at the store … Savannah shows up, wants to talk to him.
DAVID TOLBERT (police interview): I didn't know she was gonna come up there today. And I told her I had to go into work.
The store had four security cameras.
DAVID TOLBERT (police interview): We were going over the stuff for the inspection and she came in and ...

Police say Savannah Tolbert had driven her blue Kia Sorento to the store that day. She was sporting a new, short hairstyle and is seen on camera arriving at the store shortly before 2 p.m. David Tolbert, wearing a black baseball cap and a hoodie, greets his wife with a hug. Moments later, they leave the store together.
You can't hear the audio, but you can see David and Savannah talking outside the store.
Investigator Jeff Kreiter: He tells her to wait. It'll be about 30 minutes before the inspection is done.

David Tolbert walks back to the store, alone. Then, one of the cameras from inside the store captures a glimpse of Savannah Tolbert walking across the parking lot. Investigators believe she was walking to the Tesla and that it was the last time Savannah was seen alive.
Then, about 20 minutes later, David Tolbert grabs a Yeti-style coffee mug and is seen leaving the store.
Investigator Jeff Kreiter: He goes out to the … Kia that … she drove there in, she's not there. He says she must have went to the Tesla maybe to watch a movie.

DAVID TOLBERT (police interview): My car has a screen. You can go in and watch TV on it and stuff like that. … I went over there and hit the thing to get in my car and just sat down and looked over and she was there.

Investigators quickly learned everything they could about the couple. After almost two years of marriage, they had been living apart for several months. And according to David, Savannah had been struggling with mental health issues.
INVESTIGATOR KREITER (police interview): What is this she is diagnosed with?
DAVID TOLBERT: She had depression, anxiety.
Investigators had been told by first responders that the gunshot wound was in the back of Savannah Tolbert's head, near the left side, but the gun had been discovered in her right hand.
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON (police interview): Is she right-handed or left handed?
DAVID TOLBERT: She's right-handed.
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: She's right-handed. OK.
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: Did you see a gun on her when you got in the car?
DAVID TOLBERT: I saw it in her — in her lap.
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: If she was right-handed … why would she do this to shoot herself?
DAVID TOLBERT: Why would she shoot herself to begin with?
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: That's what we're trying to find out.
Investigators started talking to David and Savannah's friends and soon learned about a woman named Chelsea Finch.
Investigator Jeff Kreiter: In talking, uh, to everybody … David himself, Chelsea's brought up.
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON  (police interview): Who is Chelsea?
DAVID TOLBERT: Chelsea is one of my friends. I installed a Tesla charger at her house.

Investigator Jeff Kreiter: We end up calling her … and she agreed to come up and meet. And it just so happened she ended up being there at the same time … David was in the interview room … 'Cause we kind of wanted to see that reaction when she got the news.
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON (police interview): … we're here to talk to you about David and his — his wife, um, Savannah.
CHELSEA FINCH: OK.
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: Well, she's deceased.
CHELSEA FINCH: Gotcha.

Investigators say Finch, an aerospace missiles engineer, appeared calm when she learned Savannah Tolbert had died. She told investigators she had met Savannah a few times at a vape shop where David Tolbert worked.
CHELSEA FINCH (police interview): And then I — he was my go-to person for Tesla because he had a Tesla and I was given no tutorial on how to operate my Tesla.
Investigators soon learned David Tolbert and Finch had been doing a lot more than talking about their Teslas.
CHELSEA FINCH (police interview): We said I love you and stuff like it's — it was definitely —
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: Intimate.
CHELSEA FINCH: Yes.
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: OK … you understood that he was still married. Did you press him to get a divorce?
CHELSEA FINCH: No.
Investigator Jeff Kreiter: … she said that they were in love, uh, that David was gonna leave, uh, Savannah for her …
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON (police interview): Do you — do you love him?
CHELSEA FINCH: Yeah, I do.
Police say it is unclear whether Savannah Tolbert knew her husband was having an affair. Finch revealed in her police interview that David had told her his wife might be moving back to their home.
Chelsea Finch: So, if she moved back in, in my mind, that's my hard cutoff.

Even if Savannah Tolbert had moved back home, David Tolbert, it seems, had already decided to end their marriage. He had given her divorce papers, but she had not signed them. Three days later, those papers were found in the red Tesla where Savannah was discovered.
Savannah Tolbert's husband says she was depressed; her sister says she was scared
After Savannah Tolbert's death, her sisters were still reeling from the devastating news they had learned from investigators: their sister may have taken her own life.
Holly Hancock: it really wasn't a question in our mind. We knew she didn't kill herself.
April Hancock: We know Savannah wouldn't do something like this.
Savannah was the eldest of three sisters in a close-knit southern family. Holly Hancock is the middle sister.

Holly Hancock: Growing up we were thick as thieves until somebody stole a hair bow or a T-shirt … when you think about the kind of family dynamic with sisters, I would say we fit that to a T. We always had each other's backs unless we were at each other's backs.
Savannah and her sisters suffered a life-changing loss as children when their mother took her own life.
Anne-Marie Green: What sort of impact did that have on your family?
Holly Hancock: I would say that brought us closer together as sisters and it really put Savannah in the spotlight for that older sister role who also assumed kind of the lead female in the family.
And Savannah shared her story on social media.
SAVANNAH TOLBERT VIDEO: Today is, um, world suicide prevention day … this is a really personal topic for me. As some of you, most of you probably know, my mom passed away by suicide when I was 16 …
According to her family, Savannah had a keen sense of awareness and understanding when her family and friends were going through a rough patch. April Hancock is the youngest sister.

April Hancock: She's always a listening ear. … If you're having a hard time, if you're going through something talk about it … Don't bottle it up, don't hold it in. Like, I'm here. I'll take the time.
And time with her family was a priority for Savannah. She doted on daughter Avery, from a previous marriage.
Avery Foster: She loved to craft. She got me into crafting, um, she liked to go on walks. She liked to spend time outside.
Anne-Marie Green: She liked to make videos too …
Avery Foster: … she just liked to video everything …
Anne-Marie Green: What do you think Savannah saw in David?
Holly Hancock: I think that he knew how to say the right words.
David Tolbert told investigators he met Savannah in 2013. The couple got married in 2020.
Holly Hancock: She did a 1920s — roaring 20s-themed wedding … she had down to the tiniest little detail planned out …
Anne-Marie Green: What was David like at the wedding?
April Hancock: Cloud nine.
Anne-Marie Green: Were you all happy that she was getting married?
April Hancock: We were happy that she was happy.
After the wedding, the newlyweds started a food truck selling mac and cheese. The business fizzled out after seven months.
In May 2022, April and Holly Hancock, who lived in Tennessee, noticed a change in Savannah Tolbert's demeanor in their phone conversations.
Holly Hancock: She seemed a lot more flighty to me …
She didn't seem like herself, they say, but they didn't know why.
April Hancock: … more on edge.
Holly Hancock: Skittish. Yeah, on edge … she didn't have as much to say.
Savannah's ex-husband Andy Foster, Avery's dad, knew Savannah's mom had taken her own life. He gave Savannah his word that he would keep an eye on her mental health.
Andy Foster: I always made her a promise … if I ever noticed any shifts that I would step in and intervene … and I did that …
He lived in the Huntsville area and when he observed Savannah was struggling —

Andy Foster: I called her sister and I called her dad … and I'm like hey, this is what I've noticed with Savannah. Something needs to happen. She needs to go somewhere. I'm — I'm not related to her, so I can't send her anywhere. I need help from you guys.

Savannah's sisters later learned she had voluntarily checked herself into a Birmingham, Alabama, hospital around July 2022. They say they don't know why she was admitted, but she stayed three days. It was something David claims Savannah didn't want to share with her sisters.
Anne-Marie Green: David's not calling you?

Holly Hancock: No. … We proceeded to call Dave after that and asked him for well-being and also why he hadn't told us any of this and his response was that Savannah wanted him to keep it a secret, um and that he was trying to honor her wishes.
At the time, Savannah's daughter Avery was living with her dad. After Savannah was discharged from the hospital, she was readmitted to another hospital in early September for a longer stay.
Holly Hancock: Dave brought her to Nashville where I live and I met him at the hospital to help check her in together,
Anne-Marie Green: What was she like at that point?
Holly Hancock: Very childlike, very timid. … She was scared. She did not want to stay there.
David Tolbert told investigators during his police interview about Savannah Tolbert's behavior at the time, including how, he says, she avoided going anywhere near their home.

DAVID TOLBERT (police interview): … she thought there was black mold at the house and the house was haunted, and uh, there was a lot of stuff wrong with the house and she couldn't stay there … with me not being there because it was either too loud or too quiet and both of them were terrible for her.

Savannah was discharged from the hospital, moved out of the marital home, and moved in with her grandparents. On Nov. 15, 2022, the day she died, investigators learned Savannah had an appointment with her therapist.
Anne-Marie Green: Was Savannah depressed?
Holly Hancock: Honestly, I would say no. What … I observed from her was not depression. It was — she was scared.
Back at the police station, David Tolbert was tested for gunshot residue, known as GSR, in the interview room      .
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON (police interview): You told me you didn't wash your hands, right?
When investigators got the results –
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: Those GSR tests, they pop blue for GSR on your hands.
DAVID TOLBERT: I don't know what GSR is.
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: Gunshot residue.
DAVID TOLBERT: Oh.
While investigators waited for Savannah's autopsy report, they learned there was no gunshot residue found on her hands.
David was free to leave after his interview. But before he left the police station,  investigator Kreiter presented a hypothetical scenario.
INVESTIGATOR JEFF KREITER (police interview): So there's — the investigator that is out there right now, looking at the cameras, the surrounding buildings, not gonna find footage.
DAVID TOLBERT: Not a bit.
INVESTIGATOR KREITER: Of — of you —
DAVID TOLBERT: Doing nothing.
INVESTIGATOR KREITER: — shoot — shooting your wife.
DAVID TOLBERT: I did not shoot my own wife.
Investigators Kreiter and Hayden showed us what they had discovered — another valuable clue to learn what really happened that day.
Anne-Marie Green: So you're looking for some camera, something to see what happened with Savannah. What do you guys discover as you look around?
Investigator Greg Hayden: We searched the entire area … and luckily we were able to find this camera right here on Valley Pools.
The security camera was perched near the roof of the Valley Pools store – about 100 yards away from the scene.
Anne-Marie Green: The Tesla is parked all the way over there.
Investigator Greg Hayden: That's correct … The camera's pointing directly at us in front of the business right there.
Investigators believe David Tolbert didn't know about that camera. It was far away, but close enough to capture video of his red Tesla.
Multiple cameras provide clues. What will the Tesla tell investigators?

In the days following Savannah Tolbert's death, her sisters Holly and April Hancock, continued to cope with their grief. But David Tolbert never reached out to them. Their relationship with their brother-in-law was strained from the beginning.
Anne-Marie Green: How did David kind of interact with your family?
April Hancock: Very boastful … always bigger and better and can outshine and outdo …
Holly Hancock: He did always have a better story. He had a better car than you.
Avery Foster: So, I never really saw him a lot … unless it was like, like a weekend and it was really late.
Savannah's daughter Avery first met David Tolbert when she was about 5 years old. She said her new stepdad was somewhat strict – especially about what she watched on TV.

Avery Foster: … and he'd be like … "well this is not a kid show. You can't watch it with us. You gotta go to bed" … and I was like alright … feel like I'm being pushed off because I don't — like I don't get to hang out with y'all. … I feel like a family is supposed to watch TV together, even if it's a little late on a Saturday night or something.
The family says David Tolbert made an impression, wearing three-piece suits and carrying a wad of cash.
Anne-Marie Green: Was he wealthy?
April Hancock: … no. I think he just liked to portray that.
He also liked luxury cars — especially Tesla, says investigator Jeff Kreiter.
Investigator Jeff Kreiter: He- — he loved that Tesla … probably — it was probably his prized possession.
And that Tesla – where David said he found Savannah's body – would become a focus for investigators, as would that parking lot security video from the Valley Pools store.
Investigator Greg Hayden: I went back to when he first pulled that Tesla up and we watched from when he got there …
Anne-Marie Green: The thing with this Valley Pools video is that it's far away and it's really grainy and even kind of … when you zoom in, it almost becomes more obscured.
Investigator Greg Hayden: It pixels out.
Despite the poor quality, investigator Greg Hayden had a hunch it could provide another valuable clue – adding to the video police had gathered from the store where David worked.
Investigator Greg Hayden: You can clearly see his face, what he has on which is a dark sweatshirt …
When the store video was synced up with that grainy parking lot footage of David's car —
Investigator Greg Hayden: An entire scene is put together.
— it provided a video timeline for investigators to follow from the moment Savannah arrived at the store.
Investigator Greg Hayden: Right here you'll see Savannah walking … and you'll see her walk over to the edge of the counter where she greets, uh, David at and they hug here.
Anne-Marie Green: And then what happens?
Investigator Greg Hayden: Then he'll eventually walk her back outside, which will be to her car.
David returns to the store. Then, shortly after 2:15 p.m., the Valley Pools video shows an unidentified person standing near the Tesla just as Savannah is seen approaching the car's passenger door.

Investigator Jeff Kreiter: You see this black blur right here … This is Savannah. You see the door open. And then she will get inside the passenger side seat of the Tesla … We know this because … there's no other blurs or blobs or whatever you want to call it get near that passenger door. You never see that passenger door open again.
The unidentified person walks away, and about 20 minutes later another person approaches the driver's side of the Tesla.
Investigator Greg Hayden (pointing to security camera video): That's him right there.
There's a tree partially blocking the view, and you can't see a face, but investigators say that's David Tolbert near the car.
Investigator Jeff Kreiter (pointing to security camera video): … which is this pixel-y type blob at the car.
David Tolbert told investigators when he opened his car door, he discovered Savannah dead in the front passenger seat. But investigators didn't believe he was telling the whole story.
Investigator Greg Hayden: I think that when he opened that door … pulled out that weapon and she moved away from him and he shot her.
Investigators say David Tolbert moves away from the car. A short time later the Tesla's taillights flashed on and off.
By now investigators were highly suspicious David had something to do with Savannah's death, so they called him in for a second interview.
He arrived at the police station with Chelsea Finch. She is by his side, rubbing his back.
Anne-Marie Green: Why was Chelsea there in the interview room?
Investigator Jeff Kreiter: She gave him a ride.
Investigator Greg Hayden: Yeah.
When Finch left the room, the interview started.
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON (second police interview): Alright Dave, how you been doing man?
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: Trying to absorb everything?
DAVID TOLBERT: I'm lost.
Anne-Marie Green: So what happened in the second interview?
Investigator Jeff Kreiter: That's when he brought up this, uh, toy cannon or whatever.
After David Tolbert's car was seized for evidence, authorities discovered a mini cannon, a collectible for hobbyists, in the trunk.
Investigator Jeff Kreiter: … It would fire off like small projectile-type stuff. … it's something that could have — would've had gun powder on it.
Investigators already knew the retired corrections officer had tested positive for gunshot residue on the day Savannah died.
Investigator David Kreiter: He was smart enough to know that was … you know, an issue of course he had a law enforcement background, um, so he needed to come up with a way to explain it.
David Tolbert claimed the cannon had fallen off the seat in his car and that he had moved it to the trunk. Kreiter believes David cooked up that story to justify the gunshot residue on his hands.
Investigator Jeff Kreiter: The problem would be when we got the video from Valley Pools, you can see him pull in ... At no point does he go to passenger side or go to the trunk ...
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON (second police interview): When did you go to the trunk of that car?
DAVID TOLBERT: I want to say I did it as soon as I pulled up because that's when it fell.

Police believed David Tolbert's Tesla could provide additional evidence, especially when they discovered the car's exterior cameras – a feature known as Sentry Mode – where a series of cameras can record and monitor what's happening outside the vehicle.
Investigator Jeff Kreiter: So obviously we're interested in that …
David Tolbert was asked about it during his initial interview.
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON (first police interview): Does your car automatically record?
DAVID TOLBERT: It does if I had my jump drive in it.
According to investigators, David Tolbert was an ardent user of Sentry Mode.
Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: He wanted Sentry Mode to always be active.

We wanted to know how Sentry Mode works, so we asked Rich Benoit an electric vehicle specialist and the host of the YouTube channel "Rich Rebuilds." He demonstrated on a Tesla similar to David Tolbert's car.
Anne-Marie Green: So how many cameras are on, say, a Tesla like this?
Rich Benoit: On this specific Tesla, it has eight cameras, but only four are used for Sentry Mode …
Anne-Marie Green: OK, and it's recording now?
Rich Benoit: It's recording right now, yes.
Benoit showed us where the cameras are located.
Rich Benoit: This is the first camera for Sentry Mode right here.
Anne-Marie Green: Mm-hmm.
Rich Benoit: And then we have one at the back where the backup camera would be. So, right there.
Anne-Marie Green: Oh, yeah.
Rich Benoit: Yeah, there it is.
When the camera detects motion, it starts recording.
Anne-Marie Green: How much do the cameras see? Can it — can they see all around the vehicle?
Rich Benoit: You see the entire 360 view around the vehicle. So you see from both sides, you see from the rear, and the cameras in the front.
Anne-Marie Green: Where is the data stored?
Rich Benoit: That's a very good question. So for this specific car and how this is set up, the data is stored locally on the vehicle on a USB drive.
Prosecutor Ben Gibbons says David Tolbert was known to have his car's Sentry Mode turned on.
Asistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: He would tell people you know this is to save you, this is to protect you. Keep Sentry Mode active.
But on the day of Savannah's death?

Investigator Jeff Kreiter: Unfortunately, uh, David, um says he doesn't have a memory card in, uh, in the car to keep any data on there. … so this car that he was so proud of and has all these features, he was choosing not to use any of them, um, at least on this particular day.
Investigators believed they had a lot of the evidence that could prove Tolbert had murdered Savannah – but what they needed was the autopsy report from the medical examiner.
Anne-Marie Green: When you locate the wound in her head, tell me what's going through your mind?
Dr. Jonrika Malone | Medical examiner: What's going through my mind is, this is not right.
Was David Tolbert's mistress a motive for murder?
The circumstances surrounding Savannah Tolbert's death were highly suspicious, but to make a case for murder, authorities needed the medical examiner's report.
Dr. Jonrika Malone: The circumstances were suggestive of a possible suicide based on the fact that she is sitting in the car with the gun in her hand. …
Dr. Jonrika Malone is a state medical examiner for the Alabama Department of Forensic Sciences.
Dr. Jonrika Malone: I had to actually find the gunshot wound, which was in the back of her head, in her hairline … and so that did not ring normal to me and made me a little suspicious.
Remember, Savannah was discovered in the front passenger seat with a gun in her right hand. So, the location of the wound, in the back of her head, raised even more questions for Malone.

Dr. Jonrika Malone: It's very difficult, especially seated in a car, considering there's a headrest behind you, to be able to get your arm and hand back around there in order to do the gunshot wound to yourself.
Malone learned from investigators that there was no gunshot residue found on Savannah — so her next discovery was telling. There was no imprint from the gun's muzzle on Savannah's head.
Dr. Jonrika Malone: The barrel of the gun was not directly in contact with the skin nor was it very close to the skin.
Anne-Marie Green: Could you estimate how far the gun was from her head?

Dr. Jonrika Malone: Well, taking into consideration the different characteristics that you see in a gun .. the lack of gunpowder stippling suggests that …the gun should have been at least three to four feet away from her head at the time of discharge.
That means the gun was fired at a distance and not at close range. Malone determined Savannah had not taken her own life.
The autopsy report concluded Savannah had died from a gunshot wound to her head. The manner of death: homicide.
Anne-Marie Green: Why are you so confident that this is a homicide?
Dr. Jonrika Malone: The reason for my confidence in this is that there is no feasible way that she could have done it.
On Dec. 9, 2022, less than a month after Savannah's death, David Tolbert came into the station for a third police interview.
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON (third police interview): You haven't been back to work?
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: So, you've been doing no work?
DAVID TOLBERT: I've just been trying to make it.
Just like the two previous police interviews, David was read his rights and agreed to answer questions without a lawyer present.
Investigator Greg Hayden: When we talk to him, David, in my opinion, was all matter-of-fact … I think he was very confident … that I got these guys wooed over. They even let me go twice.
Anne-Marie Green: And what was the purpose of the third interview?
Investigator Greg Hayden: Third interview was we was gonna break a little bad news to him …
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON (third police interview): And we talked to, uh, the district attorney … and we — we told them everything, we — we showed them the videos – we — we did all this stuff, man.
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: … and their conclusion was that — to arrest you.
INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: To arrest you for capital murder.
Tolbert appeared stunned. Madison County assistant district attorneys Shea Keller and Ben Gibbons would prosecute the case against David Tolbert.
Anne-Marie Green: Why is this a capital murder case?

Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: So, in Alabama, capital murder is a murder plus something … and there are a whole list of the somethings that can, uh, aggravate a murder into capital murder. … In this circumstance, it was because Savannah was sitting inside of a car … the facts are that she was inside of a car when he shot her so it's capital murder.
Tolbert was patted down and checked for weapons.
Before investigators left the room, they asked David Tolbert if he had anything to say.
DAVID TOLBERT: I don't believe this is happening.
DAVID TOLBERT: I tried so hard to get her mental health help for months and months.

Moments later, Chelsea walked into the interview room. She had driven David Tolbert to the police station in his Tesla. Investigators do not believe she had any knowledge or involvement in Savannah's death.
DAVID TOLBERT: They're arresting me.
DAVID TOLBERT: They're arresting me for murder.
CHELSEA FINCH: … I know you didn't do it.
CHELSEA FINCH: I got you. OK?
Chelsea, holding Tolbert's hand, continued to comfort him.
CHELSEA FINCH: Babe. Hey.
CHELSEA FINCH: I need you to stay strong, OK?
CHELSEA FINCH: You pinky promised me.
CHELSEA FINCH: I got you. You didn't do this. I know this.
David Tolbert was handcuffed and taken to jail where he was held until his murder trial.
Assistant D.A. Shea Keller: So I love trying a case with Ben, because Ben is like science and facts. And I'm like what's the juice here? … Why did he do this?
Prosecutors say David Tolbert had manipulated everyone around him and wanted them to believe Savannah, who had been struggling with mental health issues, had taken her own life.
Assistant D.A. Shea Keller: This is not a case about mental health…. This is about a man murdering his wife.
And Tolbert's motive for murder?
Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: He wanted Savannah out of the way so that presumably he could be with his mistress.

No witnesses heard the gunshot the day Savannah Tolbert died and, despite the hours of video investigators had collected in this case, there was no video that could prove David Tolbert had fired the gun that killed her.

Assistant D.A. Shea Keller: As a prosecutor, your job is to seek justice from the smallest thing on a traffic ticket, all the way up to a capital murder like this case. Rarely do you have a truly innocent victim. … And that's what Savannah was.

Two-and-a-half years after Savannah Tolbert's death, a jury would have to decide if Tolbert had killed his wife in broad daylight without a single witness while she sat in the passenger seat of his red Tesla.
The case against David Tolbert
David Tolbert went on trial in May 2025 in Huntsville, Alabama. There were no cameras in the courtroom. We spoke with two first-time jurors selected to decide Tolbert's fate.
Andrea Mendoza | Juror: My name's Andrea Mendoza … I am a mom. I'm 26 years old. I'm currently a college student who is studying vet medicine.
John Grzybowski | Juror: My name is John … I'm a retired rocket scientist.
Anne-Marie Green: The setup in the Huntsville courtroom is a little different than it is in a lot of other places … the jury's kind of like in the middle of the room.
Andrea Mendoza: Yeah.

John Grzybowski: Yes … I had not heard about this shooting previously before the trial, so it was all new to me. So, I was just kind of … surprised that something this tragic had happened so close to where I live.
The case against David Tolbert would be argued by assistant district attorneys Shea Keller and Ben Gibbons.
Assistant D.A. Shea Keller: This case is about a master manipulator.
Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: I think the real him showed himself … in the Tesla when he pulled the trigger.

Assistant D.A. Shea Keller: David Tolbert was somebody who wanted out of the circumstances of his life. … He wanted out of his marriage … it's about someone using … the fact that they're suffering … mental health issues, their darkest days against them, trying to make that the scapegoat for a murder.
The prosecution's case centered around security camera video — particularly, the grainy footage of Tolbert's red Tesla.
Assistant D.A. Shea Keller: Some of the worst evidence we've ever put in in a trial …

Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: It did what it, you know, what we needed … in showing that the only two people to ever even approach that car … were Savannah, because she never left the car, unfortunately, and David, because he walks to the car presumably to find her body and then walks back in the store.
Prosecutors say David Tolbert shot Savannah Tolbert in cold blood before he walked back inside the store. And, because the Valley Pools camera was about 100 yards away from the Tesla —

Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: … you can't definitively say you can see David open a car door on the driver's side. You can't tell if it's the front door or the back door. … I think that he opened the back door and kind of ducked down and shot her.
And they believe David Tolbert had been hiding the gun in the pouch of his hoodie – and that Savannah Tolbert saw it before he pulled the trigger.
Assistant D.A. Shea Keller: I think she saw, she turned, and that's why the bullet lodges where it lodges.

David Tolbert's defense case was based on Savannah Tolbert's struggles with her mental health. Defense attorneys said she had taken her own life. And they zeroed in on medical examiner Malone's own words in her report to make that case: that because it was an active investigation, suicide cannot be completely ruled out. Dr. Malone defended her findings.

Dr. Jonrika Malone: At the time that I closed my report, there were ongoing investigations … it's easier for me to explain it in the courtroom to say, yes, that's what I said, but it doesn't change the fact that it's a homicide.
Prosecutors also called Chelsea Finch, the woman they believed was the motive for the murder, as a witness. Chelsea told the court David Tolbert wanted a future with her.
Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: … he lied to her as well.
Assistant D.A. Shea Keller: That's true.
Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: He lied to everyone about everything. She wanted to believe him.

Finch testified that she broke up with Tolbert a few months after his arrest. Prosecutors learned that after David Tolbert's Tesla was processed for evidence, it was returned to him. Before he was arrested, he took a road trip with Chelsea.
Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: He took her to Disney in that Tesla.
Anne-Marie Green: In the Tesla that Savannah died in?
Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: Yes.
The defense did not call any witnesses, and David Tolbert did not testify. He did not respond to our request for an interview. After three days of testimony, the jury got the case.
Andrea Mendoza: We wanted to all go through the evidence, but we were all pretty much on the same page.
They deliberated for about 3 hours.
John Grzybowski: We found him guilty.
Guilty of capital murder.

Andrea Mendoza: I made it, uh, a thing to look at him directly as it was happening … they were putting him in handcuffs is when he kinda like … turned a little red and looked like he was a little wobbly in the lip … it's kind of like he knew it was coming is what it felt like in my opinion …
Savannah Tolbert's family still struggles with her death. For sisters, April and Holly, her loss is also a life lesson.

Holly Hancock: I think as a family member, a lesson that we have learned is that, like, you should speak up when you're uncomfortable and things don't seem right … And even if you're afraid that you're going to hurt your family member's feelings … your intuition is something that you should trust.
Savannah's daughter Avery lives with her dad and stepmom.
Anne-Marie Green: Do you see Savannah in Avery?
April Hancock: Yes.
Holly Hancock: So much so.
Anne-Marie Green: Tell me what you see.
April Hancock: Man, all her spunk, her intelligence, charisma.
Today, she is finding her way and reaching for the stars.

Avery Foster: I hope to work for NASA and … join the astronaut program by taking that stepping stone of being a Naval pilot. … and I wanna show that there's women that can go through hard things and still make their dreams come true. … I think that drive really did come from my mom.
For Savannah's sisters, the jury's guilty verdict was bittersweet.
Holly Hancock: It wasn't a positive feeling, you know? … It's like, it doesn't bring her back …
Anne-Marie Green: Did you look at David?
April Hancock: Oh, most definitely … pay the piper. May you rot. May you rot.
David Tolbert is serving a life sentence without the possibility of parole. The prison where he's locked up is a place he knows all too well.
Anne-Marie Green: David Tolbert is a retired corrections officer. … Where is he now?

Assistant D.A. Shea Keller: Limestone Correctional Facility, the exact correctional facility where he was a corrections officer. … justice for the family and justice from our perspective is different. And that is just rich. … that is the cherry on the top for the two of us. Yes.
If you or someone you know is struggling with mental health, contact SAMHSA'S National Helpline at 1-800-622-HELP.

Produced by Marcelena Spencer. Iris Carreras  is the field producer. Michael Vele, Grayce Arlotta-Berner and Marcus Balsam are the editors. Anthony Batson is the senior producer. Nancy Kramer is the executive story editor. Judy Tygard is the executive producer.
In:

48 Hours
Murder

title: Some Florida voters with ties to Venezuela discouraged by Trump's policies
summary: Doral, Florida, has the largest Venezuelan population of any city in the country.
story: Latinos voted in record numbers for President Trump in 2024, but polling shows that voting bloc is up for grabs in the midterms.
And one region that reflects that shift is Florida's Miami-Dade County, where Latinos and Hispanics make up more than 70% of the population.
In January, CBS News met Andrea Ramos and her husband in Doral, Florida, as they were celebrating and closely following the capture of former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.
Ramos, a naturalized U.S. citizen from Venezuela, told CBS News that she credited President Trump with Maduro's capture. Doral has the largest Venezuelan population of any city in the country.
"I had such big admiration for him," Ramos told CBS News about her sentiments for the president following Maduro's arrest and extradition to the U.S.
But about nine months later, her feelings have changed.
"I feel disappointed," Ramos said. "I feel, in a way, betrayed."
While disappointed with the economy, it is the Trump administration's immigration crackdown that has led Ramos to sour on Mr. Trump and the Republican Party.
"Overall, I'm not feeling like the law is being respected," Ramos said.

According to a CBS News Battleground Tracker poll released earlier this month, 60% of Hispanic likely voters said they were likely backing congressional Democrats in the upcoming midterms, compared to 39% who said they were likely backing Republicans.
That marked a considerable shift from 2024 CBS News exit polls, which found that 51% of Hispanics voted for Democrats, compared to 46% who voted for Republicans.
In the same new poll, 59% of Hispanic likely voters found that the Trump administration was trying to deport more people than they had expected, compared to 51% of all likely voters.
Asked in the poll about the Trump administration's focus on deportation, 59% of Hispanic likely voters responded that it was too much, compared to 49% of all likely voters.

Stephanie Caro's family-owned coffee shop in Doral is among many local businesses that have seen a decrease in foot traffic and sales as masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have been photographed on the city's streets.
"I'd say there is a heightened sense of fear," Caro said.
Some local business owners have said they're concerned they'll have to close their doors.
"It really impacts the entire community," Caro said. "People are scared to leave their houses. They're changing their daily routines."
Doral voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, driven by Venezuelan Americans who fled Maduro's socialist regime.

But ICE has increasingly targeted asylum seekers who have pending cases and active work permits, and Mr. Trump's close relationship to Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez has impacted his support in Doral.
When CBS News asked Doral's Republican Mayor Christi Fraga three times if she still supported Mr. Trump, Fraga refused to give a direct answer.
"There is a lot of things that I support, and there's also questions that I've raised," Fraga told CBS News.
Ramos remains undecided on who she will vote for in the upcoming midterms. On that question, Fraga also declined to advise her constituents to vote for Republicans.
Said Fraga, "Vote your conscience."

title: DOJ demands that some California counties set aside alleged noncitizen ballots
summary: Federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California demanding that local officials set aside and verify ballots that the Justice Department said may belong to noncitizens.
story: Federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California on Friday demanding that local officials set aside and verify ballots that the Justice Department said may belong to noncitizens, according to the Los Angeles County registrar and a letter obtained by The Associated Press.

The letters are the latest escalation in a legal battle between California and President Trump's Justice Department, which has recently focused on the state in its efforts to root out noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. Data shows illegal voting by people who aren't U.S. citizens is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races.

Earlier this month, the federal government targeted L.A. County and the California Secretary of State's office in a lawsuit that aimed to block them from counting the votes of more than 20,000 people who it alleges are "likely" noncitizen voters. A hearing on the case is scheduled for Tuesday.
The Trump administration on Friday asked the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals to rule on the lawsuit barring a decision from the district judge assigned to the case. They set a deadline for Saturday.

Now, according to the L.A. County registrar's office, at least 18 counties across the state have received similar letters. They were given a 48-hour deadline to provide identifying information corresponding with ballots that the federal government believes were sent to noncitizens illegally registered to vote. The letter requests that county officials also sequester any ballots where citizenship cannot be verified.
"Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy," said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli.
The Justice Department is asking counties to send information about the voters it suspects are noncitizens including Social Security numbers, ID information, a copy of their registration and more.

That information can help the government and state quickly assess each person suspected of illegally registering to vote, said the letter sent to San Bernardino County voting officials. The letter says the government's list of suspected noncitizen voters includes 1,133 people from the inland Southern California county.

However, the California attorney general's office said the letters contained errors. For example, Mendocino County officials received a list of people who were not residents there, according to a court filing by the state.

Department of Justice spokeswoman Kiersten Pels emphasized in a statement on Saturday that the department is explicitly "not requesting a purge, cancellation of registrations, or any programmatic action."
Instead, Pels wrote, federal officials are asking for collaboration to "ensure the most secure election in California history."

California's secretary of state and the Los Angeles County registrar have opposed the federal government's demands. In legal filings, lawyers for California say the request threatens to delay the certification of the vote and undermine the legitimacy of the November midterms. They have also argued that the federal government's data is unreliable and that their demands risk disenfranchisement of citizens.

Voting is underway in California, with the state's more than 23 million registered voters receiving ballots in the mail earlier this month. The state said in legal filings that over 330,000 mail-in ballots have already been counted.
"All of this is simply meant to raise huge doubts about the integrity of this election," said John Tuteur, the registrar of voters for Napa County in California's wine country.

Tuteur said that two uniformed Department of Homeland Security officers delivered a letter to his office late on Friday afternoon. The letter included the names of 42 people whom the federal government accused of being noncitizens illegally registered to vote. There are roughly 86,000 people registered to vote across the county of over 130,000 people, Tuteur said. Approximately 11,000 people had already cast a mail-in ballot as of Friday.
Tuteur and other election officials who spoke to The Associated Press on Saturday said they have already started to count ballots that have trickled in from the state's 23 million registered voters.
"We're not changing anything we're doing. We're proceeding with the election," he said.
He said his employees and his relatives were worried about what could come next.
"My family's upset, worried about what's going to happen to me," he said.

The letters on Friday came on the heels of a statewide sweep by federal authorities earlier in the week, where 28 people from the list of 20,000 were charged with illegally registering to vote. Some were also charged with illegally voting and lying on naturalization paperwork. Those charges could lead to years in prison.

The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division has filed 31 lawsuits in an effort to force states to hand over unredacted copies of their voter rolls. The division has said it wants to ensure states are keeping clean voter lists, but it has since acknowledged that it also intends to share the data with the Department of Homeland Security so that the lists can be screened for noncitizens.

Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division, sent letters to all 50 states in July threatening to take criminal action if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls.
So far, the Justice Department has lost 26 of those cases, and has not achieved one legal victory to date.

"This is NOT A DRILL: Donald Trump and Todd Blanche are trying to interfere in California elections," Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla of California said in a statement Friday. "Trump's DOJ has not provided any evidence for their claims of massive voter fraud. They've admitted that the data they point to is inaccurate and unreliable. No matter how many lawsuits they file or how many election officials they threaten, they do not have the authority to interfere."

title: In Ohio rally, Obama blasts Ramaswamy, GOP over controversial Acton ad
summary: Former President Barack Obama took aim at gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has doubled down on an advertising campaign featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Amy Acton.
story: Former President Barack Obama on Saturday seized on what he described as cruelty and indecency coming from President Trump and his Republican allies, stepping into one of the nation's ugliest midterm fights as he worked to rally Democratic voters in battleground Ohio.

Obama took specific aim at Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has doubled down on an advertising campaign featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Amy Acton. Mr. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have also defended the ad, even as Republican leaders across Ohio, including Gov. Mike DeWine, have called for its removal.

"In recent days, we've seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to," Obama said of Ramaswamy, noting that Acton has "spoken movingly about her painful childhood and all she's experienced: abuse, neglect and homelessness."

"There's a decency we should expect out of our public officials," Obama continued. "And I don't know what's happened where the standards of behavior are so low that somebody could run an ad like that."

Obama, 65, remains the Democratic Party's best motivator nearly a decade after leaving the White House. He campaigned in Michigan later Saturday night, lending the Democratic Party his star power in Midwestern battlegrounds that will help determine the balance of power in American politics next week.
Obama shared the stage with Acton and former three-term Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is looking to unseat Republican Sen. Jon Husted.

Although Ohio has become more reliably Republican, it's been a hotly contested battleground this year. Mr. Trump and Vance have both visited the state in recent weeks to drum up support for Husted and Ramaswamy. And the controversy over Ramaswamy's ad has ratcheted up the already high temperature.

Ramaswamy has defended his decision to press ahead with the ad as fair game. Mr. Trump aggressively defended the ad, which has emerged as a national flashpoint in the midterms' final days, as he voted in West Palm Beach on Saturday.

"This is a disgrace," Mr. Trump said. "The mother said that Amy Acton is a liar and she's no good. And you know what? I don't think you can get a better reference on that." He added that if his own mother had said anything bad about him, it would be front and center.
The Ramaswamy campaign video features Acton's birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her "a liar" and insinuating she has mental health issues.
Acton says her mother "was not well" and her stepfather "was not a good person"

Acton, Ohio's COVID-19-era health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child. Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather, Arthur's husband, was indicted on a charge of rape involving Acton.

The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur failed to show for a court appearance and became a fugitive. Donna Arthur remained married to him until his death in 2004.

"I hope that everyone is seeing all the facts," Acton told CBS News ahead of the rally. "The facts are: I was removed from custody from my mom. She was not well. From even a very young age, my brother and I experienced a lot of abuse and neglect, even before my stepfather. But my stepfather was not a good person, and it got worse then. He was indicted in a grand jury. He was a fugitive, and they left together. And she obviously decided to leave with him. There's a lot out there of what has happened to her since, but I have not seen her since I was 12 years old in a courthouse. So this is a sad story."
Acton told CBS News that "we all know that that was a line crossed too far," adding that "no one running for office should endure something like this."
She went on: "But I can tell you, my childhood made me who I am. It made me stronger. You know, I'm not the only one who's gone through a thing or two in my childhood."
Appearing on stage before Obama, Acton spoke as if addressing Ramaswamy directly.

"My opponent has chosen to exploit, intentionally, my childhood to save his stumbling campaign, but it's not going to work," she said. "Decency still matters." She added: "Mr. Ramaswamy, you are not just out of touch, you are out for yourself and you are a danger to my state. Apparently there is no low to which you won't stoop."
Obama blasts White House for "chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence"

In Ohio, Obama also called out Mr. Trump's inability to lower costs, a key campaign promise, noting that the president has instead focused on building a new White House ballroom and helipad on the South Lawn.

"I don't know if you've noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovation," he quipped. "He should be on HGTV." He went on: "There's gold everywhere. He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."
The former Democratic president acknowledged that the nation has Mr. Trump for another two years, until his term ends. But voters are not stuck with Mr. Trump's allies, he said.

"We're not stuck with a spineless Congress and Republican governors who are handling lawlessness and carelessness and cruelty and indifference for working people," Obama said. "After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in modern times, you get a chance to say enough is enough."

After wrapping up in Ohio, Obama headed to a rally in Detroit for Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official who is working to unite the Democratic base in Michigan after winning a divisive primary by less than a percentage point. El-Sayed is running against former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican.
Obama will headline a rally in Georgia next week with Sen. Jon Ossoff and candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms. Mr. Trump is slated to speak in Georgia Saturday.

title: President Trump, first lady vote early in person in Florida
summary: President Trump and the first lady voted in Florida before he jetted off to Georgia for a campaign rally.
story: President Trump and first lady Melania Trump cast their votes for the midterms in person in Palm Beach County, Florida, on Saturday.

Mr. Trump, who has been on the campaign trail this week, voted at the Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections building before jetting off to Georgia for a rally in support of Republican Reps. Mike Collins and Rick Jackson.
Earlier this week, the president said he prefers to vote on Election Day. However, he is registered to vote in Palm Beach County.
In recent elections, Mr. Trump has voted by mail. The president, however, is critical of widespread mail-in voting.
Saturday is the first day of early voting in Florida, which runs from Oct. 24 through Halloween.
Mr. Trump's Election Day plans are not yet clear. He didn't answer when reporters asked this week what he'll be doing that day.

The president is traveling most days to hold rallies for Republicans. He was in South Carolina Wednesday night and in Iowa Thursday night. On Friday night, he delivered remarks in Fort Myers, Florida.
Ahead of Saturday's rally in Perry, Georgia, Mr. Trump said Collins and Jackson are "two incredible people."

"Their opponents are Radical Left Lowlifes and Lunatics who want to Take Away Your Guns, Open Your Borders, Allow Men To Play In Women's Sports, and have Transgender nonsense for everyone. I Won Georgia in a Record Vote. See you later!!!," he wrote on Truth Social.

title: Hero dad who stopped Oregon school shooter shares his story
summary: 36-year-old Kaylub Giamanco shared his story with Oregon Public Broadcasting a week after the school shooting that killed three children and a teacher.
story: Kaylub Giamanco, the man praised as a hero for fatally shooting a gunman at a school in Bend, Oregon, last week, is speaking out for the first time about the moments leading up to the shooting and how he is grappling with the aftermath.

The 36-year-old carpenter, whose two daughters attend Silver Rail Elementary School, told Oregon Public Broadcasting that it was happenstance that he was passing by the school at that moment. He said he had decided to go home for lunch that day instead of eating the food he had packed.

As he drove by the elementary school, he saw a "man in black" holding a long gun and shooting at a vehicle. At first, he thought it was a prank, but then the shooter threw the gun over the school fence before climbing it.

"That's when panic fled into my brain and that's when I opened my center console and said, 'No. No. No. No,'" Giamanco said in the interview. In the console of his truck was a .40-caliber handgun he rarely used.
He said he grabbed the weapon's magazine from another compartment, drove into the school parking lot and saw the shooter walk across school grounds.

"I just was in full panic, like, 'No, there's children, there's babies in there,'" he recalled. "I told my Siri to call 911." He said the dispatcher had questions for him, but he didn't stay on the call.
"I said, 'I'm sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die,'" Giamanco said.
He described trying to stay out of sight as he followed the gunman.

"I heard him fire two shots into the doors," Giamanco said. "That's when I started hearing children pleading for their lives and then I started hearing gunfire and I just started army crawling faster and faster and I told myself this is probably the last thing that I'm ever going to do."

Giamanco said he crawled in through a broken window, staying on his knees until he reached the special education classroom. He said he saw a teacher struggling with the shooter. He said he swung the door open and fired.
"He (the shooter) was scrambling for his weapon," Giamanco said. "I looked at him and I shot him two more times to make sure that he couldn't move because I was afraid of him shooting anybody else."

Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek was among those who praised Giamanco's bravery, saying he "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life." Police Chief Mike Krantz also credited the teacher who tackled the shooter and fought to take his gun, which "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed."

Police later identified the shooter as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II. The attack killed three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher. A 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded.
"I didn't save everybody. I didn't get them all."
After police and first responders arrived at the school, Giamanco went back to his truck, emptied his weapon and called his wife and then his mother.

"She was just like, 'OK, baby, calm down. You did the right thing. You're a hero. You saved lives.' And I was just like, 'I didn't save everybody. I didn't get them all,'" he recalled of the conversation with his mom.
His mother, Kenda Freeman, who lives in California, told CBS News Sacramento that her son "has a genuine heart and he loves his community and his family and his children."
A week later, Giamanco told Oregon Public Broadcasting that when he goes to bed at night, he replays that day in his head and wonders if he could have stopped the shooter sooner.
"I relive, I see faces, I hear voices, I hear screams," he said.
"It was split-second decisions while gunfire was going off, while children were losing their lives."
He grew emotional when talking about the families who lost children.
"I want to apologize for not saving their babies," he said. "The gratitude for saving people's children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn't save."

In the days after the shooting, Giamanco sought to avoid the limelight, putting out a brief statement expressing gratitude to first responders and the community. However, he told Oregon Public Broadcasting he's now decided to share his story.

"I've always wanted to change the world, but I've felt small. I'm just a carpenter from Bend, Oregon. I was a nobody other than to my friends and family," he said. "I feel like if I'm going to have a voice, then I'll be damned if I'm not going to use it to change this world, to make it a better place."
He said he hopes to help raise funds for local schools to improve their safety.

title: 2 ex-FBI officials charged with lying about Hunter Biden laptop probe
summary: Two former FBI agents have each been charged with one count of lying to Congress about the investigation into Hunter Biden's laptop.
story: Washington — Two former senior FBI officials are facing criminal charges for allegedly making false statements to Congress during testimony in 2023 about the bureau's investigation involving Hunter Biden's laptop.

Nikki Floris, 46, a former intelligence analyst in charge in the bureau's Washington Field Office, and Bradley Benavides, 56, the former deputy assistant director at the FBI's Counterintelligence Division, each appeared in court on Friday in Washington, D.C., where they were presented with a copy of a criminal complaint charging them with one count each of lying to Congress about their roles on the Foreign Influence Task Force during the 2020 election, specifically the FBI's Hunter Biden investigations.

A statement of facts prepared by the FBI and filed with the complaint alleges that Floris made false statements to Congress on July 19, 2023, and Benavides allegedly did the same that September. Their alleged false statements pertained to "their awareness of involvement in the FBI's investigations into Hunter Biden," it said.

"The evidence further establishes probable cause to believe that Floris and Benavides made these statements for the purpose of concealing [the Foreign Influence Task Force's] engagement with and communications about the Hunter Biden investigations and impeding the congressional investigation," it said.

The decision by the U.S. Attorney's Office in D.C. to charge the pair in a criminal complaint stemming from three-year-old allegations is highly unusual, and both their defense attorneys and the magistrate judge who presided over Friday's hearing and unsealing raised questions about the decision.

"The alleged conduct happened years ago. The government has had the information about this for years," said Ron Safer, an attorney for Benavides. He asked Zia Faruqui, the magistrate judge at Friday's hearing in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, to immediately schedule a preliminary hearing "as soon as humanly possible" to review whether there was adequate probable cause that a crime was committed.

The politically charged case was also unsealed just about two weeks before the midterm election — a fact that may raise questions by DOJ veterans about the timing of a case involving testimony to Congress that occurred more than three years ago.
Faruqui said he thought the manner in which the case was charged seemed "strange" and he rejected a request by prosecutors to delay the preliminary hearing for two weeks or more.
He ordered the parties to return at 11 a.m. on Tuesday.
"This is the Sword of Damocles hanging over their heads," he said. "This will follow them for the rest of their lives."
Former President Joe Biden's son Hunter has long been a target of President Trump and his allies.

Hunter Biden was extensively investigated by the FBI over his business dealings in Ukraine with the energy company Burisma, and the contents of his laptop after he left it at a repair shop in Delaware.

Former Attorney General Merrick Garland eventually appointed a special counsel to handle the investigations. Hunter Biden was tried and convicted on three felony gun charges. He pleaded guilty in a separate criminal case to three felony tax offenses and six misdemeanor tax offenses.
He was pardoned by his father shortly before his father left office, and was never charged with wrongdoing in connection with the allegations involving his overseas business dealings.
The charges
The criminal complaint unsealed on Friday said an FBI unit chief told investigators in October 2026 that Floris and Benavides both had oversight roles into the various Hunter Biden probes.

The complaint focused on an FBI counterintelligence operation by the Foreign Influence Task Force known as "Round River," which, it said, was focused on collecting "derogatory informant reporting on, among other things, Hunter Biden, to flag the reporting as Russian disinformation."
Floris served as the deputy assistant director of the FITF from mid-2019 through mid-2022, while Benavides served as its section chief from mid-2019 through the 2020 election, it said.

"Witness accounts and contemporaneous documents from December 2019 through September 2021 show that Floris and Benavides knew about and were actively involved in the FBI's investigations of Hunter Biden. FITF hosted classified briefings for the agents and prosecutors on the Hunter Biden case in which Floris and Benavides  were active participants," the complaint said.

When Floris later testified to the House Judiciary Committee in July 2023, the complaint alleged she lied about her involvement in the Hunter Biden investigation and the role of the Foreign Influence Task Force.
In one exchange cited in the complaint, she was asked: "Did you have any involvement in the Hunter Biden investigation?" to which she responded, "I did not," the complaint said.
In another exchange cited, it said she was asked: "Was there ever a discussion at the FITF about Hunter Biden?"
"No. At least not with me," she responded, adding: "And again, there's a whole team below me, so whether or not conversations happened, I don't know, but I personally did not have any conversations."

In the September 2023 interview with Benavides before the House Judiciary Committee, the complaint said he told investigators he only learned some of the details about the investigation into the Hunter Biden laptop from Wikipedia when preparing for the hearing.
"When did you learn that there was an ongoing criminal investigation related to the laptop?" it says he was asked.
"The Wikipedia page," he said.
When pressed whether he had any knowledge about the matter during his time at the FBI, the complaint alleges he said, "No."
The complaint also cited a congressional staffer who was present for both interviews. That staffer told investigators the testimony from both officials appeared to be "materially untrue."
An FBI employee also later told investigators that he personally spoke with Benavides about the laptop and discussed reviewing its contents.

"Floris testified that she had no involvement in the Hunter Biden investigations. In reality, she was in frequent communication with the case team for over a year during which she both sent and received information about Hunter Biden," the complaint said.
"Benavides' testimony followed a similar pattern," it added.

The complaint and accompanying sworn statement also allege that Floris and Benavides were involved in reviewing materials to help prepare a script for a defensive brief, which aims to warn someone that he or she may have been the subject of foreign disinformation.

On Aug. 6, 2020, they provided two separate defensive briefings to Sen. Charles Grassley and Ron Johnson related to potential Russian disinformation, it said. It also alleged that Benavides and Floris were involved in reviewing and approving a Round River report that scrutinized informant intelligence related to the Hunter Biden investigations.
Floris' attorneys said in a statement that she has been falsely accused of a crime and raised concerns about the timing of the charges.

"Nikki Floris is a patriot. She served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years. Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It's no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election," they said.

"The government's reasons for charging Nikki are as transparent as they are unjust: to push a false narrative for a shot at political points. It's another sad day for the DOJ, but we look forward to Nikki's day in court."

During Friday's hearing, James Kirkpatrick, a special assistant U.S. attorney who came from the U.S. Attorney's Office in the Western District of Missouri, appeared at the lectern and spoke for the Justice Department. He was accompanied by George Massucco, the criminal chief in the U.S. Attorney's Office in D.C.

A spokesperson for Pirro's office said that Kirkpatrick does work in the criminal division there, though an internal Justice Department directory and his LinkedIn page still listed him as being in Kansas City.

At the hearing,  after the defendants' attorneys asked for a preliminary hearing as soon as Monday,  Kirkpatrick raised concerns about such rapid timing, saying the case agent is from out of town and that he would be out of town as well.
"You have charged this case," Faruqui retorted. "So you will be spending a lot of time in town."

Kirkpatrick's LinkedIn profile has since been taken down. A spokesperson for Pirro said that Cory Jacobs, the deputy chief of the criminal division, and John Borchert, the chief of the Fraud, Public Corruption and Civil Rights Section, are also working on the matter.
This is not the first time that the Justice Department has tapped prosecutors from other districts to help on controversial cases.

Last year, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Virginia tapped prosecutors in the Eastern District of North Carolina to help with the prosecution of ex-FBI Director James Comey over lying to Congress.

That office also tapped an assistant U.S. attorney from the Eastern District of Missouri who mostly handled civil cases to work on the prosecution of New York Attorney General Letitia James, who was accused of bank fraud in connection with a mortgage.

In the Comey and James cases, prosecutors from out of town were brought in after people inside the office refused to participate due to concerns with the evidence, sources previously said. Both cases were dismissed, after a judge found the interim U.S. attorney who secured the indictments was unlawfully appointed.

title: Medicare Advantage plans cut for 1 million seniors, insurers say
summary: Two of the largest private insurers are discontinuing some Medicare Advantage plans amid higher costs and a spike in utilization.
story: Two of the largest private health insurers in the U.S. are canceling some Medicare Advantage plans for seniors, CBS News has learned.

Humana and UnitedHealthcare each said they are discontinuing the plans beginning next year, ending healthcare coverage for a total of about 1 million people who are 65 or older. Healthcare Brew first reported the insurers' moves.
Humana's decision to exit the plan will affect roughly 600,000 enrollees, according to a company spokesperson.

UnitedHealthcare also confirmed that it is closing a Medicare Advantage plan for roughly 390,000 of its members, who will have access to another UnitedHealthcare Medicare Advantage plan.

title: AI agents detected inside customer bank accounts, report says
summary: Banks have detected personal AI agent activity inside customers' accounts as experts warn about the risks of oversharing with AI.
story: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized activity from third-party AI agents operating within their customers' online accounts, according to a new Axios report.
Some of the biggest financial institutions in the U.S. say customers have given their personal AI agents, which are unvetted by banks, access to their financial accounts.

"In a lot of cases, this is just going to be customers giving their username or password to an AI agent that the bank hasn't had a chance to vet yet, that goes against the bank's terms of service," Madison Mills, senior AI reporter for Axios, told CBS News. "In other cases, in our reporting, we did find evidence that appeared to look like agents taking actions in customer accounts that were not authorized."
Examples of agent behavior that a user never approved include the AI calling a bank with a complaint without first consulting the account holder.
"So, really a nightmare of AI agent activity for banks," Mills said.

To be sure, these agents weren't going rogue or hacking customer accounts and depleting their funds, Mills said. They were largely following user instructions without the bank's permission to transact on behalf of a human account holder.
"In no way cyberattacks"

White House AI czar David Sacks responded to the Axios report, saying in a post on X that there's a clear distinction between personal AI agents that help manage users' bank accounts and hackers deploying AI for nefarious purposes.

"There's a world of difference between user-authorized agents (Muse, Instinct, Grokbot, etc.) and true unauthorized/rogue agents that could constitute cyberattacks," he said. "Most of the activity described in the Axios story appears to be the former: customers sharing credentials with agents so they can take actions on their behalf."
Sacks added, "This may violate bank terms requiring humans to log in themselves, but these are in no way cyberattacks."

He believes banks should support the use of such user-authorized AI agents, but that if banks want to limit their access, they could grant AI agents "read-only" permission, meaning they could view a user's spending and other bank activity but couldn't take autonomous actions.

Under such circumstances, an agent could view your purchases and opine on whether you're spending too much money eating out, for example. But it couldn't make a purchase on your behalf or take any other action.
"Full write access (with user credentials) is a different risk category and should be approached carefully," he said.
Mills noted that it's an industrywide problem facing dozens of financial institutions as they race to curb AI agents' access to customer accounts.
Banks taking action
Some banks said they're taking action to make their customers aware of the risks of sharing their credentials with AI.

"Customers should not give their username and passwords to anyone. We support secure, customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers to meet customers' needs while keeping their accounts safe," a Chase spokesperson told CBS News.
JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon expressed concern about AI agents taking actions in customers' accounts on the company's Oct. 13 earnings conference call.
"We're not going to allow just any outside agents to come in inside the company because it's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," he said.
Charles Schwab's CEO earlier this month said the company has been blocking unauthorized agents, according to Reuters.
A spokesperson for Morgan Stanley said it had not observed any unauthorized AI agent activity across its platforms.
Bank of America and Wells Fargo did not immediately respond to CBS News' requests for comment on the matter.

title: More people now use GLP-1s to lose weight than for other health issues
summary: Growing usage of GLP-1 drugs for weight loss is reshaping how consumers shop for food and clothes, according to consulting firm EY-Parthenon.
story: More Americans are now taking GLP-1 drugs to shed some pounds than to treat diabetes and other health conditions for which the medications were originally prescribed, new research shows.
Roughly 54% of people taking semaglutide medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy do so to lose weight, overtaking the share of people who use them for other medical reasons, according to EY-Parthenon.

Meanwhile, as usage of GLP-1 drugs for weight management surpasses other medical uses, more consumers are changing how they eat and shop, the strategy consulting firm found in a survey of nearly 15,000 people, including 3,602 current or former GLP-1 users.

For example, people taking the drugs typically consume fewer unhealthy foods and less alcohol in favor of healthier products. Sixty-three percent of GLP-1 users say they have reduced their consumption of sweet snacks, while 57% say they eat fewer salty snacks, according to EY-Parthenon's research.
Food makers, grocery chains and other retailers are adapting to those changes in consumer habits.

"We are finding that manufacturers and retailers are making more room on store shelves for GLP-1-diet-specific foods, or protein-enhanced items, and smaller portion sizes," Don Johnson, a principal in EY-Parthenon's consumer strategy practice, told CBS News. "Some consumer packaged goods makers thought this was a blip or fad. Now I don't hear that. Everyone accepts that this is a structural change that's not going away."
Smaller sizes, fitted styles

Growing use of the drugs for controlling weight is also changing how consumers shop for clothes. In the apparel department, EY-Parthenon researchers found that consumers taking GLP-1s are gravitating toward smaller clothing sizes and more fitted clothing, swimwear and athletic wear.
"You're losing a lot of weight on the drugs, so you're needing to buy differently," Johnson said.

EY-Parthenon found that 72% of GLP-1 users sized down in clothing after rapidly losing weight, requiring a wardrobe refresh. Roughly half of users increased their spending on fitness services, such as gym memberships, while 46% switched apparel brands.

GLP-1s have become accessible to a broader swath of consumers, driving increased adoption for weight loss, according to EY-Parthenon. The drugs are today available in more forms, such as a pill, and are also more affordable, leading more younger, lower-income and male consumers to use the drugs, according to the research.

Changes in public policy are also helping drive wider usage of the drugs. A Trump administration agreement last year with GLP-1 manufacturers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk lowered the cost of Ozempic and Wegovy to between $150 and $350 per month, down from roughly $1,000 per month. The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program also provides eligible Medicare beneficiaries with access to GLP-1 drugs for $50 a month.

GLP-1 drugs also could have clinical value in helping people deal with other issues, some researchers think. Experts at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania are embarking on a study to see if the drugs can deter risky financial decisions.

In a first-of-its-kind study, the researchers will examine how GLP-1s influence the body's reward system, a network of brain structures that reinforces certain behaviors, to see whether the drugs suppress temptations such as luxury purchases, gambling or other activities that people often find hard to control.
