title: More than 1,000 arrested in France as protesters and police clash
summary: While demonstrations throughout France were largely peaceful, police reported clashes with protesters Saturday evening.
story: Police made 1,314 arrests in nationwide protests in France, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said Sunday, after demonstrations over the high cost of living and the country's education system earlier in the day remained largely peaceful.

Nuñez 53 officers were hurt in marches. He said on Saturday marches "passed off well" in cities, but police officers found themselves confronted with "an extremely elevated level of violence" from "ultra-left" groups later in the day. Nuñez said some shops and businesses had been looted, but "the scale was far smaller" than a week earlier, when some 3,000 businesses were damaged or looted.

He said police acted more rapidly and conducted more pre-demonstration checks. Businesses and shopping centers had also been better protected. Earlier Saturday, the interior minister said police had confiscated weapons including metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana and airsoft weapons, he said.

The French Interior Ministry said about 410,000 people participated in about 298 protests around the country. Union organizers from the General Confederation of Labor put the number at around 800,000.  An explanation for the discrepancy was not immediately available.

Some confrontations were reported between authorities and demonstrators in several cities, but as of Saturday evening there had been no repeat of the major street violence and rioting that erupted amid similar protests last week.

Nuñez previously said that French authorities were preparing to maintain order this weekend by maintaining up to 70,000 officers nationwide along with assets including helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons.
Nuñez said authorities will remain "on high alert" overnight and into Saturday.
Clashes break out in Paris after largely peaceful march

Paris had prepared for unrest, with shops boarded up and events including those related to the NFL's first French football game canceled, but authorities described the atmosphere in the city as "calm."

Thousands gathered at the Porte d'Italie on the city's southeastern rim for an authorized demonstration. The march had originally been set for the Bastille, near the city's center, and was changed to the more remote Porte d'Italie at the last minute. Union representative Murielle Guilbert told reporters that it was "scandalous" that Macron had forbidden protesters from demonstrating "where we wish to demonstrate," but participants complied with the change.

The front of the march ended without incident. Some chanted "We are not happy" as they peeled away from the Porte de Vincennes. Police said 110,000 people participated in the event, while union members put the number at 250,000.

As the evening went on, clashes were reported between police and demonstrators, the Agence France-Presse reported. Nuñez said that "several thousand radical activists" had "gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters."
Clashes between protesters and police lasted about two hours, he said.

The Paris prosecutor's office said 64 people, including six minors, were arrested and 40 were placed in police custody. Most arrests concerned suspected weapons offenses or participation in a group preparing violence or property damage, the office said. More than 3,000 were stopped and checked by officers, police said.
Protesters march against far-right gathering

In Orleans, thousands of people marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party. Le Pen is launching her campaign to succeed Emmanuel Macron as France's president. Elections will be held in six months, and surveys show Le Pen is best-placed to win. Demonstrators in Orleans protested both Macron and Le Pen.

"Macron resign. Le Pen in prison," the crowd yelled, according to the AFP. Police put their numbers at 11,000, while organizers said 26,000 took part. About 50 organizations, including labor unions, left-wing parties and student groups, had called for a protest against Le Pen's nationalist, anti-immigration party.

Some placards seen at the march referenced a shooting in Trappes, a Paris suburb, that left one person dead and several others injured across several locations. Macron called the rampage a "racist terror attack." Prosecutors are investigating the shooting as a terrorist incident.
French media reported that the protest against the congress ended peacefully early Saturday afternoon. The gathering is expected to continue through Sunday.
Protesters and police clash in smaller cities

Demonstrations had been banned in the southeast city of Lyon, but about 150 protesters near the city's center briefly tried to block a road. Police fired tear gas to disperse the group. Tear gas was also used to break up a group of around 1,000 people gathered in the south of the city. Street fires were also reported.

A police helicopter was seen flying over the city, and security forces, armored vehicles and riot police vans were patrolling. A 21-year-old student, who spoke to the Agence France-Presse on the condition of anonymity, described authorities as "really mobile."

In the western city of Nantes, thousands of protesters broke through police lines to enter the city center, the AFP reported. Officers used tear gas and a water cannon to try and disperse them. Some on the fringes of the demonstration threw projectiles and aimed fireworks at officers.
Police said about 17,000 attended an event in Marseille. Officers fired tear gas during clashes with several dozen people near the march's endpoint. Street fires were seen in the city.
Tear gas was also deployed in Clermont-Ferrand, Bordeaux and Strasbourg, police said. Nuñez said one person was seriously injured in Clermont-Ferrand, but did not provide any details.
In the city of Toulouse, a 20-year-old man reportedly had fingers blown off, Nuñez said. He did not provide more details about the person, their condition, or how they came to be injured.

Nuñez said that in the southern cities of Cannes and Montpellier, authorities saw far-right activists who claimed they were there to protect businesses or sought confrontations with "ultra-left militants." He said it was the first time authorities witnessed this phenomenon.

In Nice, where demonstrations had also been banned, 11 people were arrested after far-right extremists fought with demonstrators downtown, regional authorities said. Water cannons were also used in the city.
Organizers call for Halloween demonstrations

One group of protesters, the Yellow Vests, said they would hold another round of protests on Oct. 31. The Yellow Vests emerged about eight years ago as a loosely organized group that staged disruptive protests against Macron.

Organizers called for rallies and a sit-in outside parliament and city halls nationwide, condemning the "authoritarian drift" of Macron's government and urging citizens to stand up for "public freedoms."

The demonstrations have been ongoing since September, when high school students in the southeast of Paris protested for better conditions. The unrest quickly spread across the country as people took to the streets to demand relief from rising living costs.
More protests spread across Europe
Other protests took place across Europe on Saturday, encompassing a broad range of issues including pensions, housing costs, anti-war movements, education and corruption.

Italian police said in a statement that they carried out nine arrests and briefly detained 371 people during protests in eight cities on Saturday. Of the people who were detained and taken to police stations, 110 were minors, the statement said. Police on Saturday also said they had arrested a 30-year-old man suspected of being the figure behind the "October 17 Movement," a group which had called for the protests.

Soldiers were deployed to Milan, the nation's fashion and finance capital, ahead of fresh demonstrations one week after looting and police clashes. Many stores were boarded up with wooden planks on Saturday. Others remained defiantly open after a call by the city's mayor Giuseppe Sala not to "panic."

"We want to give the message that we are not scared by these kids," said Alessandro Buhne, 30, who works at the Philipp Plein menswear shop. "Tourists are scared of this situation so we want to give the signal that you are safe if you enter our store."

Italy Premier Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters.
In Rome, authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up patrols around key sites. Some protesters briefly broke into the Colosseum, officials said.
Police "managed to isolate and contain the violent fringes, with balance and professionalism," Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi said, according to Italian news agency ANSA.
"In Italy there can be no room for those who delude themselves that they can act with impunity," he said.

Several hundred students demonstrated peacefully in the historic city. Organizers of peaceful events sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and their hands visible.

In Albania's capital of Tirana, riot police used water cannons to subdue large groups of protesters. Some of the demonstrators threw projectiles at police, the AP reported. A separate protest organized by the opposition outside the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama turned violent earlier Saturday, with some activists lighting fires on the street. The demonstrators are mainly high school and university students, demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting corruption in the education system. A broader anti-government movement is calling for Rama's resignation.
In Spain, thousands of retirees and others marched through central Madrid to demand that public pensions aren't meddled with.
Protesters in Lisbon, Portugal, are expected to march across the city Saturday to demand affordable housing.

title: 1 arrested after fire at Hitler's Eagle's Nest mountain retreat
summary: Police said firefighting efforts were hampered due to local conditions.
story: A suspect has been arrested in Germany following a fire at Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, known as Eagle's Nest, German police said.
Authorities were alerted to a fire at the Nazi leader's mountain residence on the peak of Obersalzberg at approximately 9:15 p.m. local time on Friday, Upper Bavaria South police said in a statement.
The building, also known as Kehlsteinhaus, was "completely engulfed in flames" when firefighters arrived, police said, but no one was found inside and no injuries were reported.
Fire trucks had some difficulty accessing the site "due to the local conditions," authorities added.

"Shortly after the fire broke out, a suspect came into the focus of investigators," the statement said, adding that the cause of the fire is now under criminal investigation and one person was taken into custody.

The 33-year-old suspect, a German citizen who has ties to the Berchtesgaden area but doesn't currently live there, prosecutors said, has been questioned, The Associated Press reported. They said he showed signs of mental illness and he was being sent to a psychiatric facility, but they also would look into the possibility of a political motive in view of the building's history.
There were no current indications that anyone else was involved, police said.

At an elevation of 6,017 feet, Hitler's Eagle's Nest was completed in 1938 and occasionally used by the Nazi leader as a temporary seat of government. The site was spared from Allied bombing during World War II, largely preserving its original state.

Since then, it has become a popular tourist attraction, which also operates as a restaurant and beer garden. According to its website, the Eagle's Nest is "one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hitler era" and it "stands for the insanity of the regime."

Bavaria's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, indicated to reporters in Berchtesgaden that the Eagle's Nest would be restored. But what the site will look like in the future will be a matter for discussions with local officials, historians, preservationists and others.
"We're not going to leave a ruin there," Herrmann said, according to the AP, adding, "I think we will be able to find a sensible solution."
The minister stressed "it is important that we continue to do the work of remembrance."

title: Elon Musk says SpaceX throttled Ukraine Starlink speeds over drone strikes
summary: SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink internet service has become the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations.
story: Elon Musk said on Saturday that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, disrupting operations that the country relies on to defend itself against Russia.

Musk's admission on social media came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine's access to Starlink and Starshield satellite links has been restored to the speeds it had before restrictions that disrupted front-line operations for more than a week.
Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Musk-made satellite internet system that Kyiv has relied on for years to counter Moscow's attacks.

"The speeds are now where they need to be," Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that restoration began overnight and were sufficient by Saturday morning, improving front-line logistics and defense against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.
Musk admits he was behind Starlink's speed restriction

Before Musk's confirmation, questions persisted last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Musk-made satellite internet system that Ukraine has relied on for years to counter Moscow's attacks.
President Trump had said he didn't make the call, while also saying Musk should not be blamed. On Tuesday, CBS News reported that Musk was behind the disruption.
In a post Saturday on X, Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX throttled the Starlink satellite internet service.

"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote. "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

But he maintained that the U.S. government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield, SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service and the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication. He also defended the role of SpaceX in bolstering Ukraine's defenses since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Restrictions imposed last week on Starshield alarmed the country's military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.

The restoration follows a new U.S. diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's southern Kherson region.
The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by Mr. Trump's reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.
Khmara credited "direct dialogue" and Zelenskyy's diplomacy with Washington, adding that the outcome mattered most "for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications."
Zelenskyy on Saturday thanked Americans and "all our partners, who took all this seriously and are really helping us."

title: Deadly shooting in Paris suburb investigated as terrorism, officials say
summary: A gunman opened fire from his car in the Paris suburb of Trappes on Friday, in what authorities described as a racially motivated act of terrorism.
story: A gunman shooting from his car killed one person and injured at least 5 others, including a 12-year-old girl, in the Paris suburb of Trappes on Friday, in what authorities described as a racially motivated act of terrorism.
President Emmanuel Macron called it "a racist terror attack" and said the suspect's statements suggested it was premeditated.

"These people were targeted because of their skin color or perceived religion, and for no other reason," Macron said following a meeting with officials and residents. "There is no place for this in France."

Prosecutors said they were investigating whether the acts targeted the "real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion" of the victims. They said they have opened an investigation for "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise."
The alleged shooter was "firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath" as he drove through Trappes and neighboring La Verriere, Trappes Mayor Ali Rabeh told broadcaster BFMTV.

"This is probably one of the first attempted mass killings motivated by Islamophobia and racism," Rabeh told reporters, the Associated Press reported. "This was a terrorist attack with racist, likely Islamophobic, overtones."

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the suspect fired "what appears to have been a military-grade weapon, or at least an automatic weapon." Rabeh called it a "miracle" that there were not more casualties. Nuñez said the gunman "clearly" committed "a terrorist crime" that may have been racially motivated.
Rabeh said the gunman targeted passersby at three separate locations, including a playground. Forensic investigators were also seen examining evidence at a gas station.

A police source told the Agence France-Presse news agency that the gunman had fired in bursts from his vehicle around 10:30 a.m. local time. Samy, a resident of Trappes, about 13 miles west of Paris, told AFP he saw a body on the ground from his window. His mother, he said, saw a gray Renault Clio car speeding by and heard "loud bangs."
The alleged shooter was arrested in the nearby town of Coignieres. Nuñez said the attack lasted just under 15 minutes and was stopped by five officers from the anti-crime brigade.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on X that the case was "very serious" and that "all resources of the security forces and the judiciary are fully mobilised." Macron said "the nation is standing with" the victims of this "terrible ordeal."
Suspect had booby-trapped apartment, investigators say
The suspect has been partly identified as Kevin T. He is 39 years old. The National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office said Saturday that his detention has been extended.
Investigators said the suspect had booby-trapped his apartment with gas bottles and electrical wires connected to a timer. He also had tear gas grenades in his car, officials said.
A source close to the investigation told the AFP that a copy of Adolf Hitler's "Mein Kampf" was found in the suspect's apartment. A Bible and Quran were also found, the source said.

The prosecutor's office said Saturday that "three additional individuals" from the suspect's "family and circle of friends" were placed in police custody on Friday evening and overnight. The office did not say why those individuals were placed in custody.

The AFP reported later Saturday that four members of the suspect's family and circle of friends were arrested and were being questioned by investigators. A source close to the case told AFP that the suspect's parents were among those under arrest.

The office also said the suspect's criminal record includes four prior convictions, all of which had been legally expunged. The office did not say what those convictions were for or when they occurred.
Deceased victim identified as MMA fighter
The deceased victim was identified as Pengo Bossio Wangi, a 26-year-old man of African origin. He was an up-and-coming mixed martial arts fighter.

Hundreds of people rallied Saturday at the spot where he was killed, as other protests swept across France. The demonstrators held placards that called for "justice" and led a moment of silence honoring Wangi.
"It could have been anyone. He opened fire on Blacks, Arabs. He knew the majority of the population here in Trappes is Muslim," a local shopkeeper of North African origin told AFP.

Wangi's family said the shooter was known to authorities, and demanded to know whether he had been properly monitored before the incident. In a statement released by the family's lawyer, they called for an investigation into potential failures on the part of the authorities and "to exhaustively establish the path that led to (the shooter's) radicalisation."
Multiple injured, including 12-year-old girl
Officials initially said four people had been wounded, but Rabeh told reporters there were five, including three who were very seriously injured, with their lives in danger.
A 12-year-old girl was seriously wounded after being shot eight times, but is in stable condition, the mayor of La Verriere, Nicolas Dainville, told the AFP.
The injured victims have not been identified. Rabeh said that one of the wounded, "in critical condition, is of North African origin."
France on edge after street violence and protests

The shooting came with France on edge following riots that erupted amid mass protests over the cost of living, which saw some of the worst street violence in recent years. Demonstrators, including students, labor union members and activists from France's "Yellow Vest" movement, took to the streets again Saturday across the country.

French police have maintained a large presence to maintain order. Dozens of arrests were reported, and some groups were tear-gassed. Resources including elite police units, helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons have been deployed.

In the city of Orleans, thousands of people marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party. About 50 organizations, including labor unions, left-wing parties and student groups, had called for a protest against Le Pen's nationalist, anti-immigration group. Some placards seen at the march referenced the shooting in Trappes.

"Racism kills. The far right kills," a lawmaker from the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party, Mathilde Panot, said at the rally near the spot of the shooting. Demonstrators also protested against Macron's policies and called on him to resign.
Le Pen called for a "relentless" investigation and said it was "despicable" if racism was the shooter's motive.

title: German man arrested for allegedly driving U.S. teen to die by suicide
summary: The 18-year-old German was arrested in Hamburg on Thursday, accused of being the indirect perpetrator of murder and grievous bodily harm, prosecutors say.
story: German police, acting on an FBI tip-off, arrested an alleged online sadist accused of driving a 14-year-old U.S. girl to hang herself, prosecutors said Friday.
The 18-year-old German was arrested in Hamburg on Thursday, accused of being the indirect perpetrator of murder and grievous bodily harm.

FBI Indianapolis Special Agent in Charge Timothy J. O'Malley said in a statement that their office worked with the Fort Wayne Police Department to provide information to the German police to help advance the arrest. The Fort Wayne Police Department said in a statement that its Homicide Unit identified a suspect who contributed to the juvenile's death.

"Anyone who targets or exploits a child should understand this: There is no safe haven from justice. It doesn't matter where you live or where you try to hide. The FBI will work with our partners around the world to find you and hold you accountable," O'Malley said.
The suspect was linked to an online group called "Nefarious Maniac Kult" or "NMK," part of a global network known by the labels "764" or "COM," the Hamburg public prosecutor's office said.

From September 2024 to September 2025, the FBI has seen a 300% increase in nihilistic violent extremism cases — many involving the 764 group, said FBI Director Kash Patel. The group 764 lacks a specific ideology, but members openly encourage self-harm and violence and encourage victims to produce videos documenting acts of self-harm or child sexual abuse material.

Between September and October, the suspect, then aged 17, allegedly "exerted influence" via the social network Discord over the girl from Indiana state whom prosecutors described as "psychologically fragile".

The suspect allegedly pressured the girl to cut herself and write the letters "NMK" on a wall in her own blood, and had her send him video recordings of these acts. A few days later, she hanged herself in her bedroom, prosecutors said.
The suspect allegedly sought a video recording of her death, hoping to gain status within the group or to secure entry into it.

title: U.K. police confirm it received letter with claims against Meghan's father
summary: On Friday, it was reported that Meghan's father, Thomas Markle, is under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child sexual abuse materials.
story: A letter making a "number of claims" against the father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was received by the Metropolitan Police in 2019, a Scotland Yard spokesperson confirmed to CBS News on Saturday.

Police said they passed the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess "for their awareness," however, the details of the allegations made in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.
On Friday, it was reported that Meghan's estranged father, Thomas Markle, is under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child sexual abuse materials.

A spokesperson for the Philippine National Police told CBS News in a statement Saturday that they launched an investigation after Markle's personal items were turned over to law enforcement by his son, Thomas Markle Jr.

"At this point, investigators are looking into the nature and origin of the materials and whether these may be connected to any violation of law," Col. Allen Rae Co said in a statement. "U.S. authorities have also offered assistance should Philippine authorities determine that their support is needed as the investigation progresses."

The British tabloid The Sun was the first to report the allegations against Markle Sr. The report said the younger Markle allegedly discovered child abuse materials in storage boxes at his father's home in the Philippines.
The Daily Mail reported Friday that Markle had denied the allegations against him.

Meghan, who recently moved back to Britain with her husband Prince Harry and their children, said in a statement sent to CBS News on Friday that she was "deeply distressed" by reports about her father. She said she had been aware of the allegations against him since 2018 and that the allegations were shared with U.K. authorities at the time.

"In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," her Friday statement said.
Meghan said she had distanced herself from her father in an effort to protect her children.

"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them," she said.

Responding to Saturday's developments dating the letter to 2019, a spokesman for the duchess told CBS News partner BBC News that "any discrepancy of a few months" was "an understandable consequence of that passage of time."
Scotland Yard said Saturday that Met Police will be reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and deciding whether to refer itself to the police watchdog.

title: Rubio calls on Cubans seeking "positive change" to work with CIA
summary: The CIA posted a video on X showing the steps needed to contact the intelligence agency.
story: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on Cubans seeking "positive change" to work with the CIA, the latest ploy in the growing efforts from the Trump administration to remove Cuba's communist regime from power.

"To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba - now is the time," Rubio wrote Friday on X. "The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA."

Shortly afterward, the CIA reposted Rubio's message and a similar call in Spanish for Cubans to work with the agency. A video was posted alongside the message showing the steps needed to contact the intelligence agency.

A strict U.S. embargo and sanctions seeking to put pressure on Cuba's communist government have led to prices of basic goods skyrocketing and decreased access to medical care for its citizens. Cubans reported waiting in bread lines for hours and others reported lining up to see a doctor.
Last week, the U.S. government announced additional economic sanctions on Cuba's state-run bank, saying the institution had ties to Iran.

President Trump said on Friday during a campaign rally in South Florida that "we'll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran." He was referring to the U.S. Navy warships deployed near the Strait of Hormuz.

Mr. Trump added: "Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We'll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They'll raise up their hands, and then we're going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal."
Cuba's government has pushed back, with Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla responding Friday on X, saying: "We reject any threats stemming from U.S. ambitions toward Cuba."

title: Iran has "increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," intel chief warns
summary: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned in a memo to Secretary of State Rubio that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," and the plots have "reached advanced stages."
story: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.

The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East, and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.

The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent.

Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.
Axios was first to report on the memo.

The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported.

"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a U.S. official told CBS News on Friday. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official also told CBS News this week that the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats.

Houthi militants have stepped up drone and missile attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeting oil infrastructure and airports. One strike on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport earlier this month killed at least a dozen people, including a U.S. citizen, and injured hundreds more.
Last weekend, U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries warned Americans to exercise caution due to Houthi attacks.

Although the U.S. and Iran have refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, President Trump has not ruled out restarting hostilities after next month's midterm elections. Iran has also continued to take responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
At a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump suggested the U.S. could launch another operation against Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement.
"We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," the president said, invoking the name of the U.S. military campaign launched in February.

title: Meghan "deeply distressed" as dad faces child abuse material probe
summary: Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, is facing a probe in the Philippines over alleged possession of child sexual abuse materials.
story: London — Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, said in a statement sent to CBS News Friday that she was "deeply distressed" by reports that her father, Thomas Markle, is under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child sexual abuse materials.

Meghan, who recently moved back to Britain with her husband Prince Harry and their children, said she had been aware of allegations against her father since 2018, and that those allegations were shared with U.K. authorities at the time.

"In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," her Friday statement said.
At this time, it is understood that the Metropolitan Police has not and is not currently investigating Thomas Markle.

"We are aware of media reports that officers from the Met's Royalty and Specialist Protection Command were involved in the passing on of a letter in 2018," a Metropolitan Police spokesperson said. "We are undertaking enquiries internally in an effort to confirm this."
Meghan said she had distanced herself from her father in an effort to protect her children.

"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them," she said.

The British tabloid The Sun reported Thursday that Thomas Markle, who has been estranged from his daughter for years, had been reported to authorities in the Philippines by his son, Thomas Markle Jr., after the younger man allegedly discovered child abuse materials in storage boxes at his father's home in the Philippines.
The Daily Mail reported Friday that Markle had denied the allegations against him.
"I have never downloaded anything like that in my life," he was quoted as telling the newspaper, as well as dismissing the allegations as "sick lies."

According to the Mail, Thomas Jr. made the discovery while his father was in the United States being treated for a stroke and blood clot. The son initially saw some of the materials after turning on an old cell phone at his father's home in the Philippines, and he subsequently reported the materials in July to an FBI hotline, as well as the National Center for Exploited and Missing Children and state police in Pennsylvania, according to the newspaper's report.
Philippines state media confrimed Friday, in a post shared on Facebook, that an investigation was underway.

"The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Friday said it is investigating reports involving an octogenarian American national who left child abuse videos and photos in his home in Cebu province," the state-run Philippine News Agency said.

A Filipino justice official said the department's anti-trafficking task force was investigating the matter and it confirmed that Thomas Markle Sr. was the subject of the investigation, according to the PNA report.
Meghan said in her statement that her "sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children."

summary: Cody Johnson walked away from a Nashville record deal after executives told him to ditch his cowboy hat, then spent a decade proving them wrong.
story: Cody Johnson talked to Fox News Digital on the iHeartRadio Music Awards carpet, and admitted his pre-show ritual is "pretty simple."

"They wanted a baseball cap, which I have nothing against, but it was the approach. It was the 'you're great, but once we change you, you'll make it.' And it pissed me off," he said in an interview with "CBS Mornings." "I tipped my hat and said, 'Thank you for your time.'"

summary: David Chokachi reveals the Andrew Huberman-inspired ice plunge and 3:30 a.m. routine that got him camera-ready for his return to "Baywatch."

After climbing out of a dark place following an arduous recovery process due to Achilles tendon ruptures, Chokachi said that he "found a higher operating system" within, and became hyper-focused on optimizing his brain chemistry to benefit both mental and physical health.
'BAYWATCH' STAR BRANDY LEDFORD SHARES FITNESS SECRETS AT 57, SAYS SHE'S 'NOT READY TO HANG UP MY BIKINI YET'
David Chokachi admitted he's more fit now than when he worked on the original "Baywatch." (Getty Images/Backgrid)

He cited neuroscientist Andrew Huberman's approach to health as an influence on his own routine and noted that former Navy SEAL DJ Shipley also helped shape his mindset.
WATCH: 'BAYWATCH' STAR DAVID CHOKACHI CREDITS EARLY-MORNINGS, TWO-A-DAY WORKOUTS FOR PEAK FITNESS

And it works, I'm telling you," Chokachi said.

In the pursuit of personal challenges, Chokachi doubled down with prepping to be on-screen once again playing a role that made him a global superstar.

"With 'Baywatch,' I realized, on the original, the more fit I was, the more stories they'd write for me, the more episodes I'd be in ... not that money is everything, but you want your character to take off," he said. "I've always been into fitness because I grew up playing sports my whole life.

CARMEN ELECTRA SAYS 'BAYWATCH' PUSHED BOUNDARIES WITHOUT CROSSING THE LINE: 'IT WASN'T PORN'

He added, "So I do that routine, and by the time I've already done that, I'm like, I'm off to the races, like, and I just go."

title: 'Vertigo' star Kim Novak plans to become compost after death
summary: Kim Novak, 93, reveals she's arranged to have her body composted after death so loved ones can plant trees, calling it "a beautiful expression."
story: Laurence Leamer has written a new book about the muses of the late director, "Hitchcock's Blondes: The Unforgettable Women Behind the Legendary Director's Dark Obsession."
Kim Novak's final act comes with a twist even Alfred Hitchcock couldn't have scripted.

The "Vertigo" star has arranged to have her body turned into compost after her death so friends and loved ones can use the resulting soil to plant trees. The 93-year-old, who is the subject of "Kim Novak's Vertigo," a documentary about her life and career, first confirmed her plans to People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA).
Novak, who lives on a ranch in Oregon, told Fox News Digital she made the arrangements "a few years ago."
'CRIMINAL MINDS' STAR MANDY PATINKIN SHARES UNCONVENTIONAL PLAN FOR AFTER HIS DEATH

Kim Novak is seen here in this undated photo. The actress confirmed to Fox News Digital she's arranged to have her body turned into compost, so friends can plant trees in her honor. (Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)

"The idea is that I get to live after I'm gone through trees," Novak said. "It's an exciting adventure because this is what I want after I pass. I want to keep living. And one thing that I've always been short on is patience. And a tree has to have patience. I will get to continue to express myself and be an observer of life. To me, it's a beautiful thought. It's given me great peace of mind because I'm going to keep growing. So I'm excited about that."
"It sounds funny perhaps, but it isn't really," she said. "I can't imagine being turned into ashes or being put under the ground. Both of those concepts are not too attractive to me."
Kim Novak arrives at Hotel Excelsior during the 82nd Venice International Film Festival on Sept. 1, 2025, in Venice, Italy. (Getty Images)
Novak isn't afraid of death, even if her plans may strike some as unconventional. The lifelong nature lover said her connection to the environment has given her peace about what comes next.
WATCH: ALFRED HITCHCOCKS BLONDES HAD A GREAT DEAL OF SEX, AUTHOR CLAIMS

"Some people may not even be aware that's a choice," Novak said. "And I know some people don't like to talk about death, or think they're going to be turned into ashes or be underground. It sounds awful. But you have a choice. You can decide what comes next."
Frank Sinatra and Kim Novak are seen here in a scene from the film "The Man With The Golden Arm," circa 1955. (United Artists/Getty Images)

"For me, this was a beautiful concept, the idea of becoming one with the soil," Novak continued. "And with compost, of course, everything grows so much better than if you didn't have it. It helps with growth. You become part of the process. It's natural, it's real, it's honest, it's pure. And I even get to choose the kind of flowers that are going to be part of my compost — forget-me-nots."

American actress Kim Novak poses with the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement trophy at a ceremony during the 82nd Venice Film Festival in Venice, Italy, Sept. 1, 2025. ( Li Jing/Xinhua via Getty Images)

Although human composting is legal in Oregon, Novak has arranged for her remains to be transported to an Earth Funeral facility in Washington state to undergo the process, known as natural organic reduction.
"I’m in Oregon, so it's not that big a deal," Novak said.
Kim Novak poses after receiving an Icon Award for her career during the 51st Deauville American Film Festival on Sept. 6, 2025, in Deauville, France. (WireImage)
"However, they’re going to have to pack me in ice in order to make it all the way to this place," she said with a laugh.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Kim Novak bites a pearl necklace in a 1950s publicity portrait. (Getty Images)
Novak acknowledged that additional options may now be available since she made her arrangements years ago.

"I'm having all of my compost, once it's done, delivered to friends and family, a bit of it," she said. "I have instructions for all of them to plant a tree or a shrub, but preferably a tree, because I look forward to keeping growing. That's what it's all about for me. I want to keep growing. This is a beautiful expression of life continuing after death."
American actress Kim Novak with British director and producer Alfred Hitchcock on the set of his movie "Vertigo." (Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)
When Novak began planning her final sendoff, she knew she didn't want to be buried or cremated. She began exploring other options.

Kim Novak delivers a speech prior to receiving an Icon Award for her career during the 51st edition of the Deauville American film festival, in Deauville, northwestern France, on Sept. 6, 2025. (Loic Venance/AFP via Getty Images)
"Here in Oregon, there was one place where I could have had a tree planted over me," she said. "However, it was only one tree. I'd like to be many trees."

According to The Associated Press, Novak was the world's top box-office star from 1958 to 1960. The outlet reported that she stepped away from Hollywood in 1966 to pursue a private life devoted to painting.
Kim Novak poses with her painting at a photocall during the Febiofest Prague International Film Festival on March 20, 2015, in Prague, Czech Republic. (Getty Images)

"Leaving Hollywood taught me that how I live my life matters," she said. "When I left, what mattered the most was being out in nature. I’ve always wanted to be close to nature and live a natural life. Painting has allowed me to continue expressing myself while out in nature. And every day of my life, I’m painting. I can’t wait to wake up each day and start working on a new painting. Sometimes, I’ll stick with a painting for months just because I haven’t fully figured out what I want to express. It’s been a wonderful way to live a life of expression."

James Stewart and Kim Novak on the set of "Vertigo," directed and produced by Alfred Hitchcock. (Corbis via Getty Images)

"Films were wonderful too," she said. "It’s just all the other stuff that went with it that wasn’t very appealing. But playing a character, becoming one with another person, that always gave me joy. When I look back at my life, I remember all the wonderful opportunities I was given to become a different, beautiful character. But even then, I was drawing too. I used to always draw the characters I was playing in my script. Every time I’d find some new feeling about my character, I would draw it and paint it."

Novak's film credits include Otto Preminger's "The Man with the Golden Arm," Joshua Logan's "Picnic," "Pal Joey" and "Bell, Book and Candle." Today, she continues to pursue painting away from Hollywood. But Novak believes her story won't end with her death.
Kim Novak attends the "Hommage A Kim Novak" photocall during the 66th annual Cannes Film Festival on May 25, 2013, in Cannes, France. (Getty Images)

"I made my decision because I want to do something good for the environment, and others can too," she said. "After we're gone, the Earth is still here, and we need to protect it. Life goes on when we're no longer here. And in some ways, this doesn't make you feel like you're dying. You're continuing to live on becoming part of the environment. It's something beautiful to look forward to, not dread."

Kim Novak poses at a photocall during the Febiofest Prague International Film Festival on March 20, 2015, in Prague, Czech Republic. (Getty Images)

"I don't want to be forgotten," she said. "I want to be remembered not just for films, but for what it made me into, what it turned me into. All the ways I transformed in life, I got to express myself in my art. And I'll continue to express myself."

title: ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ star Sarah Drew met husband leading worship at Christian youth camp
summary: Sarah Drew reveals how meeting husband Pete Lanfer at a Christian youth camp nearly 30 years ago gave her a grounding force against Hollywood's chaos.
story: The "Grey's Anatomy" alum is starring in Lifetime's "When I Said I Do," inspired by Clint Black and Lisa Hartman Black's hit duet.
"Grey's Anatomy" star Sarah Drew found lasting love long before she found Hollywood fame.

Drew opened up about meeting her husband while leading worship at a Christian youth camp nearly three decades ago. The actress, who has been married to Peter Lanfer for 24 years, credited their shared faith and strong partnership with helping her navigate the highs and lows of Hollywood. Drew and Lanfer married in 2002 and have two children.
"He's been my steady rock really and safe haven – since way before I had any success in this industry," Drew told Fox News Digital while promoting her upcoming movie, "Jimmy."
‘CHARLIE’S ANGELS’ STAR JACLYN SMITH LIVED APART FROM HER HUSBAND FOR 17 YEARS DURING THEIR 35-YEAR LOVE STORY
Sarah Drew and her husband, Pete Lanfer, have been married for 24 years. The couple met nearly three decades ago while Drew was leading worship at a Christian youth camp. (Paul Archuleta/FilmMagic)

"And we have been real partners in parenting and in being humans in this world together," she added. "And I think anytime one of us is feeling shaky, the other one is always able to provide a safe harbor and some real like rock-solid strength for the other. So, I do think probably he's my greatest grounding force."

Drew described the entertainment industry as an unpredictable business that can celebrate an actor one moment and discard that person the next, explaining why she refuses to let Hollywood determine her self-worth.

"I think that it's very easy for Hollywood to tell you who you are. And what I mean by that is, they love you one second, they've forgotten you the next. You're gorgeous one second. They're tearing you to pieces the next. You're working all the time one second, all of a sudden, you're not working anymore, and you don't know what's going on. You never know when you're gonna work again. There is no stability anywhere."
Drew said the industry's constant uncertainty makes it difficult for actors to find a sense of stability in their careers.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Sarah Drew credited her husband and Christian faith with keeping her grounded in Hollywood. She described Peter Lanfer as her "steady rock" and said her identity as a child of God matters more than her success as an actress. (Tiffany Rose/Getty Images)

"There is no place to be grounded in Hollywood. It just doesn't exist," she explained. "We are players to the whims of whoever is making the thing at the certain time and whoever's decided who's interesting or not, and I can't do anything about that."

"If I were not sure that my identity was firmly rooted first as a child of God, whose total identity is so much bigger than just who I am as an actress, if I wasn't rooted in that truth — and I know that truth to my cellular level and in my bones — I could so easily get caught up in the highs and think I'm God's gift to the Earth and then fall so miserably into I am absolutely worthless based on how Hollywood has decided to value me at any given time," she added.

Drew said her faith has helped her maintain a strong sense of identity beyond her career, reminding her that being a child of God, a wife, a mother and a friend matters more than her success as an actress.
Scene from Frank Capra's 1946 classic, "It's a Wonderful Life," starring Donna Reed and Jimmy Stewart.  (AP)

Drew stars in "Jimmy," a biographical drama scheduled for nationwide theatrical release Nov. 6. The film follows actor James Stewart's military service, his struggles upon returning to Hollywood and his eventual comeback in the 1946 Christmas classic "It's a Wonderful Life," directed by Frank Capra.
Drew stars as Hedda Hopper, one of Hollywood's most influential and feared gossip columnists.

"18 months before we started shooting, Aaron Burns …reached out to me and told me that he'd gotten the rights and had a script for this movie, ‘Jimmy,’ that he was gonna make about this incredibly important time in Jimmy's life. And I've always been a huge fan of Jimmy Stewart," she said.

Drew said Burns told her he wanted her to play Hedda Hopper, but she didn't know much about the gossip columnist. Burns told her about "this formidable and complicated person." Drew said she doesn't "generally get the opportunity to play roles like this, so I said yes before I got off the phone, before I read the script."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Sarah Drew has turned down acting opportunities because of their messages. The "Grey's Anatomy" star said she prioritizes projects that offer hope, redemption or meaningful connections over money, prestige or network affiliation. (Eric McCandless/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

The "Supernatural" star's Christian faith has also influenced her decision to turn down acting opportunities. While Drew isn't opposed to exploring difficult subjects onscreen, she said she has rejected projects that she believed lacked a meaningful message.
"I have turned down jobs because I'm like, I don't know what we're supposed to walk away from this feeling," Drew explained. "I don't see any hope. I only see cynicism. Then I'm not interested."
Drew said she has always been drawn to stories that offer something meaningful rather than leaving audiences feeling hopeless.

"I just don't understand choosing something that is only going to make people feel darker or more devastated or more hopeless, like those kinds of things," she said. "And I think that that does very much stem from my faith and from my sense of the story that sort of bubbles through my life and has all through my upbringing. And through my adult life and as a parent and as a friend and all of these things, is that I want there to be hope associated with everything that I touch or am a part of – something that you can really like look toward as a beacon of goodness in some ways."

That philosophy also plays a central role in how Drew evaluates potential projects, a process she said often involves conversations with her husband. Rather than focusing on the prestige or financial rewards of a project, Drew said the couple first considers whether the story is one she wants to tell.

Sarah Drew stars as influential Hollywood gossip columnist Hedda Hopper in the upcoming biographical drama "Jimmy." The film follows James Stewart's military service, his struggles returning to Hollywood and his comeback in "It's a Wonderful Life." It is scheduled for a nationwide theatrical release Nov. 6. (Gilbert Flores/Variety/Penske Media)

"It almost never is about what I might get paid, how fancy the project is, what network it's going to be on," she explained. "Those things are absolutely secondary to the first question, which is, 'Do you want to tell the story? Is this story that you think is going to resonate with people?'"

"I find that the stories that I'm drawn to are the ones that help people feel less alone and where someone can see themselves in a story," Drew said. "They can pick a redemption arc or a restoration arc and feel a little less alone. And they might laugh and cry and think on their way through the story of it, but at the end of it, they're like, 'Me too. I've also been through something like that. I know what that feeling is, and I feel a little less burdened and a little less alone because I have this opportunity to have this cathartic experience in a way that made me feel seen.'"

title: Sacha Baron Cohen says 'Ali G: Who Iz I?' is his last in this style of comedy, calling them too risky
summary: Sacha Baron Cohen reveals why "Ali G: Who Iz I?" will be his last over-the-top comedy, citing dangerous stunts and severe dehydration on set.
story: Comedian Adam Carolla says he was troubled by what he saw during COVID, when some performers appeared less willing to question authority or push against conventional thinking.
Sacha Baron Cohen is done starring in over-the-top comedies.

In a recent interview with The Hollywood Reporter, the 55-year-old actor confirmed that his new movie, "Ali G: Who Iz I?," will be his last in the risky, character-driven comedic style that made him famous.

"I want to do stuff that challenges me," he told the outlet. "So again, I’m not doing 'Borat 3,' which also would be incredibly challenging. Again, this movie I just did is the most challenging movie I’ve ever done, but I’m not doing more."

The actor has said he was done with this style of comedy in the past, but decided to make this movie because he is "terrified of where our society is headed" and thinks of his comedy as a way to comment on it.
Cohen says he is not going to make any more comedies like "Borat." (Taylor Hill/FilmMagic)
SACHA BARON COHEN’S RIPPED NEW LOOK FOR MARVEL ROLE HAS FANS DOING A TAKE

He explained that through his films, he can "show the extremism on both sides of the political spectrum and the danger of virtuous violence." He added that at the end of the day, he also "wanted to make the funniest film that’s ever been made."

"These really are the hardest movies to make, but I suppose I made it because I’m scared of this world of conspiracies and lies that are spread by social media and now by AI," he said. "If we don’t have these shared facts, then democracies crumble, and we can’t have a tolerant society. And to make people laugh is therapy."
Cohen's early breakthrough came in 2000, with "Da Ali G Show," and he later gained international recognition with the release of "Borat" in 2006.
He followed that up with "Bruno," "The Dictator," "Who is America" and "Borat Subsequent Moviefilm," as well as some dramatic roles in "The Trial of the Chicago 7," "Les Misérables" and "Disclaimer."

He described the final scene of his latest project as "an eight-hour continuous scene that takes place over 12 locations" with a lot of different elements, filmed as "a continual shot."

"There’s gunfire in it. There’s a medical procedure. There are drones, there are explosions, and it’s taking place in the desert," he said. "On the way to shooting it, I bumped into one of the great stuntmen and he said, 'You will go to hospital if you make this movie,' because I explained I’m wearing a prosthetic head in a fat suit. He said, 'You’ll be so dehydrated you’ll be in hospital for two weeks.'"

The "Balls Up" star explained that he hired "an endurance specialist who does the Tour de France" to be next to him throughout filming and that, despite the precautions, "a number of people went to the hospital for dehydration."

I said, 'Well, how close are you to me?' And he said, 'I’ll be with you within three minutes.' I realized that was not a good thing to do, so I pulled that scene."

summary: Michael Douglas reveals the choreography behind filming sex scenes, stressing trust and communication with co-stars before intimacy coordinators existed.
story: Michael Douglas discusses surviving stage 4 cancer, maintaining a lasting marriage and his close relationship with son Cameron. The Oscar winner has written a new memoir, "One Helluva Ride."
Michael Douglas is opening up about the "art" of filming sex scenes, revealing that the intimate moments require extensive communication and trust between actors.

During a recent appearance on "Happy, Sad, Confused" with Josh Horowitz, the 82-year-old actor reflected on filming sex scenes earlier in his career, before intimacy coordinators became commonplace on movie sets.
"There’s an art to sex scenes in films. It’s not easy to do things like shadowing people when you’re on top and this and that," Douglas said.
MICHAEL DOUGLAS REVEALS HE MADE FIVE PHONE CALLS TO FIVE WOMEN THE DAY HE CHOSE CATHERINE ZETA-JONES
Michael Douglas gets candid about the "art" of filming sex scenes. (Getty Images)
"But the big thing with sex scenes is trust," he continued. "And as long as the lady is trusting me — obviously I trust her — it’s like a dance. You’re taking the lead."
Douglas explained that actors carefully discuss each movement before filming begins.
BILLY BALDWIN ADMITS HE REFUSED TO KISS CO-STAR AFTER WEEKS OF TENSION ON SET

"You just talk it out slowly. ‘Kiss, kiss, bite. Looking at you. Is it all right to touch your breasts?’ ‘Yes.’ ’All right, I'm touching your breasts. Kiss. Kiss,'" he said. "You do it, and it’s just like choreographing a fight scene."
Michael Douglas and Sharon Stone are seen on the set of "Basic Instinct." (Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)
"You start very slowly … and then action. It makes it look like it really happens," Douglas added.
'TEACHER'S PET' STAR MAMIE VAN DOREN SAYS SHE FELT 'USED' AS YOUNG ACTRESS NAVIGATING HOLLYWOOD'S DARK SIDE
The "Wall Street" star also emphasized the importance of making female performers feel comfortable on set, particularly when they are surrounded by a predominantly male crew.
"It’s awkward enough for ladies, in terms of being mostly surrounded by a male crew and everything, especially in those days, to make sure that they were as comfortable as possible," he said.
Douglas also compared acting to working as part of an ensemble, explaining that he has always prioritized the overall quality of a project over the size of his own role.

"I've always thought your role is one small part of the whole," he said. "And so what you really need … is better actors around you. You want the best you can get because it’s the whole thing that matters."
"I’d rather be good in a little movie than lousy in a big part," Douglas added.

Michael Douglas, seen with Sharon Stone in "Basic Instinct," said that he's always seen his acting roles as being "one small part" of a much bigger project. (TriStar/Getty Images)
In his memoir, "One Helluva Ride," Douglas pulled back the curtain on the most explosive moments of his life, both in front of the camera and behind the scenes.

Douglas detailed his volatile relationship with his late father, Kirk Douglas, his son Cameron’s addiction and imprisonment, and the Stage 4 cancer diagnosis that forced him to confront his own mortality.

Michael Douglas detailed the complicated relationship with his father, Kirk, in his recent memoir. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images for AFI)
At one point, while filming "Adam at 6 A.M." early in his career, Douglas wrote that he and his married co-star, Lee Purcell, became romantically involved.

"As filming progressed, my relationship with Lee changed and we became lovers," he wrote. "Our intimate relationship was complicated by the fact that she was married, and we had to keep it a secret from the cast, crew, the people in the town we were filming in, and of course her husband. It was a passionate affair that lasted through filming."
Purcell disputed Douglas’ account in a statement to Fox News Digital.
SHARON STONE SAYS SHE 'NEARLY DIED' AFTER 'BASIC INSTINCT' OPENED THE DOOR TO HOLLYWOOD'S DARK SIDE

"This story came as a complete surprise to me. I have fond memories of Michael and our time together. However, our recall appears to differ," she said. "First, I remember the process of searching for his character of Adam after having already been hired by Steve McQueen for the role of Jerri Jo. Secondly, we had a strictly professional relationship during filming. The personal one came much later."

title: Jason Alexander admits ‘Seinfeld’ fame sent him to therapy
summary: Jason Alexander revealed on a podcast that he was in therapy while "Seinfeld" was still airing and explained why the fame was so overwhelming.
story: Comedian Tim Young tells Fox News Digital that anti-Israel protesters are interrupting the comedian's stand-up performances in hopes of getting a reaction that will spread across social media.
For Jason Alexander, fame wasn't all it was cracked up to be.

The "Seinfeld" star was a guest on Daniel Lubetzky's "Build or Break" podcast and discussed the iconic sitcom that helped shape his career. Alexander told Lubetzky that therapy was the only way he was able to cope with how much the show changed his life.
"You literally went to therapy?" the host asked.
JOHN GOODMAN ADMITS HE FELT 'FRIGHTENED' AFTER THE SUDDEN FAME HE EXPERIENCED FROM 'ROSEANNE'
Jason Alexander said he needed therapy to deal with the way "Seinfeld" fame affected him. (Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for Netflix)
"You bet," Alexander replied. "I was in therapy while it was happening."
When Alexander was asked why, he explained that the transition from the fame that "Seinfeld" brought him would be hard for anyone.
Michael Richards, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Jerry Seinfeld and Jason Alexander all starred in NBC’s "Seinfeld." (Vinnie Zuffante/Getty Images)

"The transition from successful at your job to international celebrity, let me just tell you, I don't care how well you've been raised or who you are, you're going to need some therapy," Alexander said.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Alexander went on to explain that he had one vision for himself when he was young, one dream to accomplish, and that was to make it to Broadway.
Jason Alexander leaned on therapy after "Seinfeld" ended in 1998. (Slaven Vlasic/Getty Images)
"My fantasy of a successful life for myself as an actor growing up in New Jersey was getting across the river and working on those Broadway stages. That was the pinnacle for me," he began.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

He continued, "I didn't think about television. I didn't think about film. I dreamt about a life in the theater. God gave me that starting at age 21. By the time I was 30, I'd won a Tony Award. And now they throw in my path 'Pretty Woman,' some of the other films, 'Seinfeld.' And I now live a life as an actor that I never dreamt of, never. I never thought I would have this kind of money, that I could keep my family the way I keep them, that I would have these opportunities, that I would work with the people I've met."
Comedian Jerry Seinfeld is credited as a star and co-creator of "Seinfeld." (Todd Owyoung/NBC via Getty Images)
Alexander said that when "Seinfeld" ended, his first thought wasn't to try and replace that level of success, rather he was in awe that he was able to get there in the first place.

"So, if you hit that and then that goes away, I would never go, 'Why couldn't I keep that?' I go, 'I can't believe I ever got that.' That's not what I was thinking. So for me, life gave me more than I ever dreamed of," he said. "I didn't expect that to last. I objectively could sit back. And one of the reasons that we were so adamant at the end about making money on 'Seinfeld' is because I grew up at a time when if you had a hit series on television, you never worked again. I mean, that was it."

"Seinfeld" is an American sitcom created by comedian Jerry Seinfeld and Larry David. The series premiered in 1989 and followed a fictionalized version of Seinfeld as he navigated everyday life, relationships and friendships in New York City.
Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Jerry Seinfeld and Jason Alexander are seen on the set of the last episode of "Seinfeld" on April 3, 1998. (Getty Images)
The main cast included Alexander as George Costanza, Seinfeld as Jerry Seinfeld, Julia Louis-Dreyfus as Elaine Benes and Michael Richards as Cosmo Kramer.

Often described as a "show about nothing," the series focused on ordinary situations that spiraled into comedic chaos. It ran for nine seasons and 180 episodes before ending in 1998. "Seinfeld" is widely regarded as one of television’s most influential and successful sitcoms.

title: Larry the Cable Guy knocks 'hypocrisy' in corporate America, jokes about missed endorsements
summary: Daniel Whitney, known as Larry the Cable Guy, calls out corporate hypocrisy during a podcast appearance, comparing his treatment to other popular rapper's deals.
story: Larry the Cable Guy and Nebraska legend Eric Crouch join the ‘Big Noon Kickoff’ to preview Nebraska-Indiana, discuss the Cornhuskers' ceiling, Crouch's 2001 Heisman season and more.
Larry the Cable Guy says corporate America has a double standard when it comes to choosing which entertainers are too controversial for advertising campaigns.

The comedian spoke about DirecTV, suggesting the satellite TV provider missed an obvious advertising opportunity with the slogan — "Larry the Cable Guy has switched to DirecTV." He later clarified on X that it was a "light-hearted conversation," adding that his "career has been amazing and I’m not unhappy about anything."

During an appearance on "The MeatEater Podcast," Larry recalled seeing a DirecTV commercial with an actor "back in the day" and said, "The first thing I thought was, 'Why don't they get me? Larry the Cable Guy is switching to DirecTV.’"
JEFF FOXWORTHY REVEALS HOW 'REDNECK' INSULT INSPIRED DECADES OF COMEDY

Larry the Cable Guy criticized what he sees as a double standard in corporate advertising, arguing that brands embrace entertainers he considers more controversial than himself. (Daniel Knighton/Getty Images)
A podcast host agreed with the idea, saying, "Oh, dude, that would have been genius."
The comedian agreed, saying, "It would have been huge!"
Larry said he believed there was concern that his Southern accent and edgy humor might appeal to only one slice of America and make him too controversial for a national advertising campaign.

"At the time, ‘Well, Larry the Cable Guy is only really for one part of the country, you know, ’cause of the Southern accent, sometimes he says things that are a little controversial,'" he explained of the general sentiment then.

The comedian said DirecTV missed a major advertising opportunity by not tapping him for a campaign that would have played off his famous stage name. (Getty Images)
But the comedian rejected that reasoning.

"Meanwhile, you got freaking rappers singing about killing cops" and making degrading remarks about women, he argued. "They're getting all kinds of corporate stuff. I'm, like, going, 'How am I controversial when you got … you know what I mean?"

He singled out Snoop Dogg, who has appeared in major advertising campaigns, including Super Bowl commercials. Larry emphasized that he did not fault the rapper for accepting those opportunities.

Snoop Dogg has appeared in major advertising campaigns, including Super Bowl commercials, but Larry the Cable Guy questioned why corporations embrace entertainers he considers more controversial than himself. (James Wiltshire/AFL Photos via Getty Images)
"I got nothing against Snoop Dogg," he said. "God bless Snoop Dogg.
"There's a lot of hypocrisy in corporate, who they get and who they don't get. Look, I've had a good career. I ain't worried about it. But I'm just saying that DirecTV pissed me off."

He said again he doesn't have any issue with Snoop Dogg, explaining, "I love everybody, and I'm happy for everybody's career. I'm not mad at them, I'm upset at the corporations that would say ‘you're too controversial,' but then they'll put somebody else that's even way more controversial.’"

Larry the Cable Guy questioned corporate America's approach to celebrity endorsements during an appearance on "The MeatEater Podcast," accusing companies of hypocrisy. (Isaiah Vazquez/Clarkson Creative/Getty Images)
Larry, whose real name is Daniel Whitney, built a national following with the Blue Collar Comedy Tour, alongside Jeff Foxworthy, Bill Engvall and Ron White.

title: Kate Gosselin says her kids know who she ‘truly’ is as son Collin levels abuse allegations
summary: Kate Gosselin responded to a fan on TikTok, saying her kids know who she "truly" is after Collin Gosselin's abuse allegations and memoir release.
story: ‘In the Shadow of Eight’ author tells Fox News Digital he's willing to hear from estranged mom Kate Gosselin but insists she must own up to her alleged treatment of him during his childhood.
Kate Gosselin says her children know who she "truly" is amid abuse allegations made by her son Collin.
The 51-year-old former reality star took to TikTok Thursday to celebrate her boyfriend Steve Neild’s birthday and got support from her fans in the comments section.

"Happy Birthday Steve ! Strength isn’t just about enduring—it’s about loving deeply enough to do what is right even when it costs you," one TikTok user wrote in the comments section. "Look at the beautiful life and happily ever after You have found now that You made sacrifices that no Mama should have had to make alone.
"When people attack You, it might sting for a moment, but it can never shake who You are. It only confirms that You stood your ground and remained true through it all. God is guiding You two."
‘JON & KATE PLUS 8’ STAR COLLIN GOSSELIN ACCUSES MOM OF TRYING TO ‘BURY’ HIM TO ‘PROTECT HER REPUTATION’
Kate received support from fans in the comments section of her latest TikTok. (David Buchan/Variety/Penske Media via Getty Images)
KATE GOSSELIN DEFENDS HERSELF AGAINST SON COLLIN AS HE PREPARES TO RELEASE SHOCKING NEW MEMOIR

Kate responded to the comment by thanking the fan, adding, "I needed this encouragement, and you are right," before adding that "I know who I am and my kids know who I truly am and to me, that’s all that matters."

The exchange came shortly after Collin alleged on "The View" that his sister Hannah felt compelled to say the two of them had not spoken in a year as a form of "damage control" for having participated in an upcoming Netflix documentary alongside Collin and their father.
Kate thanked her fans for their support, writing that she and her kids know who she is and "that's all that matters." (Kate Gosselin TikTok)

In a statement, Hannah wrote that she has a relationship with her mother and other siblings but has not "lived with my dad for over a year" and hasn't "spoken to Collin in close to a year." She added that she will not be making any more statements about "Collin's behavior growing up" or her experiences with him as a kid.

"All families are very complicated, and that statement sounded like a lot of the words of my mother, especially the last part. What I do believe has happened is that Hannah’s caught in the middle, and nobody deserves that," Collin said on "The View."

"I know what it feels like to have to fight to have a relationship with your siblings. I don’t have one with my siblings, and I know how much that hurts. Not only is she caught in the middle, but I do believe my mom is either leveraging finances or Hannah’s relationship with our siblings over Hannah."

In the memoir, he accused his mother of restraining him with zip ties, hitting him when he failed to perform for cameras and isolating him in the family’s basement.
